A robot that must reach many different goals needs policies that adapt to each new objective. Pei Zhou and co-authors introduce Hyper-GoalNet in a 2025 study of goal-conditioned manipulation. Keeping performance steady across diverse goals and settings is the main challenge they address.

Hyper-GoalNet uses a hypernetwork, a network that builds other networks, to generate policy parameters from a goal description. Goal interpretation is separated from state processing, so the goal decides the parameters while current observations are handled by them. The split could help robots switch tasks without retraining a fixed policy for each goal. Manipulation tasks, from grasping to assembly, are the proving ground for the method.
arxiv-2512-00285:
Mixtures of atoms and molecules form a delicate quantum system called an atomic-molecular Bose condensate. Avinaba Mukherjee and Raka Dasgupta study how such a system relaxes under Gaussian white noise in 2025. They describe the dynamics through polarization, the imbalance between atoms and molecules, and through coherence.

Relaxation times for both quantities are computed with a mean-field model and with a hierarchy that keeps higher-order correlations. The authors vary the initial polarization and the Feshbach detuning to see how each steers the decay. The results inform experiments that use noise and resonance tuning to control ultracold gases. Noise is usually the enemy in cold-atom labs, so studying its effects head-on is notable.
arxiv-2512-00385:
Splitting a three-dimensional point cloud into superpoints makes semantic segmentation far cheaper. Louis Geist, Loic Landrieu, and Damien Robert present EZ-SP in 2025, a fast and lightweight superpoint-based segmentation method. Earlier pipelines were bottlenecked by a slow partition step running on the CPU.

The authors propose a learnable, fully GPU partitioning algorithm that produces geometrically and semantically coherent superpoints much faster than prior methods. Speed matters because point clouds from lidar and scanning keep growing. Faster partitioning brings detailed three-dimensional understanding closer to real-time uses like robotics and mapping. A speedup of more than tenfold turns an overnight preprocessing step into an interactive one. Superpoints group nearby points that likely share a label.
arxiv-2512-00485:
Elliptic equations with singular terms model effects from chemical reactions to thin films, but their solutions are delicate. Fessel Achhoud and Hichem Khelifi study a class of anisotropic elliptic equations in 2025, involving unbounded coefficients and a singular right-hand side. Anisotropy means the equation behaves differently in different directions.

The authors address existence and regularity: whether solutions exist at all, and how smooth they must be. Singular nonlinearities can force solutions to blow up or vanish at boundaries, so the analysis needs care. Such results anchor work with numbers, since a computed answer means little if the problem beneath it is not well posed. Wild coefficients describe stuff whose traits can break down or blow up in places. For folks who solve such sums on a grid, the gain is peace of mind. The task they code is known to have a sound base, not just a good look.
arxiv-2512-00585:
Poisson superalgebras blend the geometry of Poisson brackets with the sign rules of supersymmetry. A 2025 study classifies the representations of the Grassmann Poisson superalgebra. The field is assumed to have characteristic different from two, so the sign rules behave normally.

The author proves that every irreducible Poisson supermodule over this algebra is isomorphic to the regular module or to its opposite. Moreover, every unital module over the algebra is completely reducible. Complete classification results like this tidy an entire corner of algebra, giving later researchers a firm list to build on. Complete reducibility means every module splits into the classified simple pieces. Representation theory asks how an algebra can act, and here the answer is short.
arxiv-2512-01085:
Wenjun Zhang, Shekhar Chandra, and Aaron Nicolson generalize medical phrase grounding in a 2025 paper. Phrase grounding links a written finding in a radiology report to the region of the image it describes. Grounded reports are easier to read, especially for non-experts who need to see what a phrase refers to.

Most current systems follow a referring-expression setup and return exactly one bounding box per phrase. Real reports often break that rule, with one finding appearing in several places. The authors' generalized approach allows the output to match how findings actually spread across a scan. Better grounding could make AI reports more transparent.
arxiv-2512-01485:
Jindi Lv and co-authors widen how language models reason through hard tasks. Step-by-step thought chains help a lot. But a single chain tends to lock onto one path. It rarely weighs other fair paths in full.

The team lets many paths grow and aid each other. Reinforcement learning guides that joint search. Soft abstract tokens let paths share sense in a smooth space. Joint search should find better answers on tasks with more than one good route. It may also cut the risk of one early slip ruining a whole chain.
arxiv-2512-01785:
Paul Desmarchelier and co-authors simulate electric double-layer capacitors with tunable electrode metallicity. Brownian dynamics tracks ions near charged electrodes. How metallic an electrode is changes ion layering a lot. Past models fixed electrodes as perfect metals or insulators.

Their description uses the Thomas-Fermi screening length inside the metal. Tuning that length spans real metals in one frame. Better capacitor models guide energy storage design. Supercapacitors need exact ion layer physics to raise density without losing speed. Screening length can be read from metal data, so the model ties to real electrode stock rather than a free fitting knob.
arxiv-2512-02085:
Lithium fluoride is a simple two-atom molecule whose energy levels twist where two electronic states nearly meet, an event called an avoided crossing. V. G. Ushakov, A. Yu. Ermilov, and E. S. Medvedev compute in 2025 how that near-meeting reshapes the molecule's rotation-vibration spectrum.

They follow the spectrum far above the first dissociation limit, into the range where the molecule can fall apart. Their ab initio calculations cover adiabatic potentials and other molecular functions across a wide span of atomic separations. The work also extracts resonances and predissociation lifetimes, telling how long excited states survive before breaking, data that spectroscopy and molecular physics rely on.
arxiv-2512-02185:
Reasoning language models answer hard questions by thinking at length, but their size and long outputs make them costly to run. Ziyan Wang and seven co-authors propose in 2025 a pruning method that trims unimportant parameters, guided by the model's own reflection on what it needs.

Pruning promises relief for deployment in resource-constrained settings, where the newest reasoning models simply do not fit. The twist here is self-reflection: the pruning decision is informed by the model's behavior rather than a blind importance score. Done well, structured pruning could bring multi-step reasoning to hardware that currently cannot afford it.
arxiv-2512-02285:
Drones can film wildlife up close, but flying too near stresses animals and ruins the very behavior researchers want to record. Jenna Kline and three co-authors present in 2025 a drone system designed to run on the aircraft itself and adapt its behavior to the animals' vigilance state.

Human operators face an attention bottleneck: they cannot fly the drone and monitor the whole group's stress responses at once. An edge-native system that watches vigilance and adjusts its approach automatically could gather behaviorally relevant video with less distraction to the animals. Better monitoring serves conservation science, where data quality and animal welfare must be earned together.
arxiv-2512-02585:
Vinod Sarky and co-authors lay out a shared database plan for energy storage materials. Batteries, solid state cells, capacitors, and hybrid devices store and supply power in compact, portable forms. Data about their materials sits scattered across papers and labs, in mixed formats that resist comparison.

A common framework for electrochemical and electrical storage data would let researchers search and reuse results. Standard records make it easier to spot trends and avoid repeating costly tests. Shared data of this kind can speed the hunt for better batteries and capacitors for vehicles and grids. Once records share one form, a search can span years of work by labs that have never met or shared a bench.
arxiv-2512-02685:
Huankun Sheng and six co-authors teach machines to split a scene into its objects without labels. Slot attention methods carve a scene into object slots, learning structure from raw images alone. Many treat foreground and background the same way, so background clutter leaks into object slots.

Their foreground aware design adds pseudo mask guidance to steer attention toward real objects. Cleaner separation improves instance discovery on real world data. Object level representations of this kind can help robots and vision systems reason about scenes as things, not just pixels. Clean splits of this kind are the first step for any tool that must count or track what it sees.
arxiv-2512-02985:
Saaketh Desai, Prasad Iyer, and Rémi Dingreville learn the elastic rules of surfaces from the behavior of the bulk beneath. Surface elasticity governs how surfaces and interfaces carry stress and hold stability. Its key quantities include surface tension, residual surface stress, and surface stiffness.

Closed form expressions for those quantities are hard to derive from atomistic data, and they depend strongly on modeling choices. The authors learn interpretable relations from bulk properties instead. Readable rules, rather than black boxes, let materials scientists design coatings and nanostructures with predictable surface behavior. Rules you can read can be taught, fought, and fixed. Rules in a black box must be taken on faith by each new team that buys in.
arxiv-2512-03085:
Smoothing data on a ring of points is a classic math task. Justin Grieshop studies one smoothing tool for that task in this 2025 work. The tool is of Fejér type, named for a known method in Fourier work, and the ring is a finite cyclic group.

Grieshop gives a self-contained account and proves a bound with clear, exact constants. Exact constants matter because users can see how large the error can be. The result fits work in signal work and number theory. It also gives students a clean path into the proof. The proof style, with all steps shown, makes the result easy to check and teach.
arxiv-2512-03385:
Voyager 1 now samples space beyond the Sun's bubble. T. A. Porter, I. V. Moskalenko, A. C. Cummings, and G. Jóhannesson study its cosmic-ray data in this 2025 work. They ask how the nearby interstellar medium shapes the spectra measured locally.

Using the GalProp code, they vary the local gas and source distributions. They look for signatures of those distributions in low-energy spectral features. Knowing the local setup helps separate true cosmic-ray traits from local effects. That aids models of how cosmic rays spread through the Galaxy. Low-energy features are the most sensitive to local gas, making them the key diagnostic here.
arxiv-2512-03785:
Transition metal oxides suit electronics and catalysis because their electrons occupy d orbitals in changeable patterns. Ellen M. Kiens and a large team show in a 2025 materials preprint how the boundary between two oxides can reset those patterns. They study lanthanum cobalt oxide, whose cobalt atoms sit in different valence and spin states depending on their surroundings.

The team layered the cobalt oxide against four partner oxides and read the cobalt states with X-ray absorption spectroscopy, checked against detailed calculations. Two partners pushed charge into the cobalt oxide, favouring one orbital occupancy, while a nickel-based partner pulled the occupancy the other way. Adding a thin spacer layer produced a low-spin state instead. Microscopy linked strain in the layers to the spin configuration. Interface design, they conclude, steers orbital filling and spin together, a lever for future oxide devices.
arxiv-2512-04185:
Axion-like particles, hypothetical light cousins of the photon, might betray themselves when a nearby star explodes. Francesca Lecce and colleagues develop that detection idea in a 2025 particle astrophysics preprint. Produced inside a collapsing star's core, such particles could convert into gamma rays while crossing cosmic magnetic fields, flashing as a short burst.

A galactic supernova would blaze brightly but happens exceedingly rarely. The authors instead target supernovae in nearby galaxies, a few per year within tens of millions of light-years. There, strong magnetic fields may convert particles more efficiently than the Milky Way's. They argue for full-sky gamma-ray monitoring, ideally paired with deci-hertz gravitational wave detectors for time-triggered searches. A decade of coverage, they estimate, could probe coupling products in territory lying below the longstanding bound from supernova 1987A, opening unexplored parameter space for very light axions.
arxiv-2512-04385:
Nan Zhou and eight co-authors present STeP-Diff, a forecasting tool for street-level air pollution built on sensors that ride on cars and buses. Moving sensors are cheap and cover wide areas, a plus for city management and healthy buildings. Yet their random routes leave data full of gaps and time mismatches. Their 2025 arXiv paper aims to forecast fine pollution maps from that messy stream.

STeP-Diff joins two ideas. A DeepONet network reads the spatial order of readings along each route. A diffusion model, guided by the physics equations of pollution spread, then fills and forecasts the field. Physics-based rules steer the cleaning steps, so outputs stay plausible even where no sensor passed. The blend held up better than plain data-driven tools in their tests. Cities could use such maps to warn residents and plan traffic with far fewer fixed stations.
arxiv-2512-04585:
Jingjing Li, Yue Feng, Yuchen Guo, and co-authors present SAM3-I, an upgrade to the Segment Anything family that follows full instructions, not just short labels. The base model, SAM3, outlines every object matching a brief noun phrase. Real users, though, give rich directions that mix traits, relations, and actions. Older setups chain outside agents to shrink such directions into labels, losing detail on the way. Their 2025 arXiv paper folds the reasoning into the segmenter itself.

SAM3-I adds an instruction-aware cascade on top of SAM3's concept grounding. It reads the whole direction, reasons about which instance fits, and draws the mask in one framework. That unity keeps fine traits that label-first pipelines wash out. Tests show sharper picks when several look-alike objects crowd a scene. Tools for photo editing, robotics, and medical imaging stand to gain from masks that honor what users actually said.
arxiv-2512-04685:
Alexander Nolte explores how flexible, even degenerate, two constructions around a theorem of Thurston can be. Thurston's work reshaped the geometry of surfaces; his asymmetric metric on Teichmüller space measures how much one surface structure must stretch to reach another. Nolte's 2025 arXiv paper first builds geodesic paths for that metric with a striking toughness. The paths stay geodesic even after small Lipschitz noise is added to nearly every coordinate of the Fenchel-Nielsen system.

The second construction concerns limit cones of representations into products of hyperbolic plane groups. For a range of copy counts, Nolte builds open sets whose limit cones are cones over explicit finite-sided polyhedra. Each construction is as degenerate as the setting allows. Such extremes probe local non-rigidity: they show where the objects refuse to be pinned down. That knowledge shapes how geometers use these spaces in dynamics and group theory.
arxiv-2512-04785:
Eranga Bandara, Amin Hass, Ross Gore, and co-authors introduce ASTRIDE, an automated threat modeling platform built for AI agent systems. Agents that decide, act, and talk with each other through language models bring fresh attack surfaces: prompt injection, poisoned context, model manipulation, and murky agent-to-agent channels. Classic threat frameworks were not drawn for these risks. Their 2025 arXiv paper extends a classic framework to cover them.

ASTRIDE grows out of STRIDE, the long-used Microsoft threat scheme. It adds a new category, A, for agent-specific attacks such as unsafe tool calls and subverted reasoning. The platform automates much of the modeling work, mapping a system's parts to likely threats. Builders can then rank fixes before deployment, not after a breach. As agents enter banking, health, and public services, threat models that speak their language become basic hygiene.
arxiv-2512-05185:
Bo Xiao, Benedikt Kloss, and E. Miles Stoudenmire extend a measurement-based simulation technique to how quantum many-body systems evolve in real time. The approach grows out of quantum algorithms that measure and reuse qubits, and of classical methods that use projective measurements to keep calculations affordable. The method weaves time and space evolution together, measuring each small region as soon as it reaches the target time. That exploits the causal light-cone structure and suppresses the growth of entanglement.

Compared with the standard time-evolving block decimation method, the simulations reach longer times for the same cost per sample. The framework also yields local measurements and correlations, both at one moment and between moments, efficiently. The traffic runs both ways: tricks designed for quantum hardware improve classical tensor-network simulation, and the classical results reveal what protocols on quantum hardware would show about entanglement dynamics.
arxiv-2512-05485:
Xiuyuan Chen and eleven co-authors assemble TeleAI-Safety, a comprehensive benchmark and framework for attacking and defending large language models. Safety evaluation has been fragmented: benchmarks typically cover attacks, defenses, or scoring in isolation, making studies hard to compare and full risk assessments laborious. TeleAI-Safety integrates all three — dozens of attack methods, defense methods, and evaluation methods, several developed by the team itself — into one modular, reproducible system.

Its curated corpus of attack prompts spans a dozen risk categories, and the authors run it against fourteen target models. The evaluations surface systematic vulnerabilities and model-specific failure cases, and they map the tradeoffs between safety and utility along with defense patterns worth optimizing. Because the framework accepts custom combinations of attacks, defenses, and evaluators, practitioners can tailor assessments to their own deployment risks. Code and results are released to seed unified safety baselines.
arxiv-2512-05685:
Yuxiao Yi, Weizong Wang, Tianhan Zhang, and Zhi-Qin John Xu attack a quiet weakness in using neural networks for chemical and nuclear reaction systems. The equations are stiff, and their variables span many orders of magnitude. Networks also favor low frequency patterns, so fast, small scale parts get learned badly. Their 2025 paper adds a scaling step, the Generalized Box-Cox Transformation, inside an earlier data driven framework.

The transform pulls quantities of wildly different sizes toward a common scale before the network sees them. In frequency terms, it shifts high frequency parts of the target down where networks learn best. Tested on six hard cases, from chemical kinetics with many species to turbulent reaction and diffusion, the method cut prediction errors by up to a hundredfold. It matched the old model's quality with about a sixth of the training.
arxiv-2512-06185:
Ankit Gupta, Christoph Adami, and Emily Dolson revisit a decade old embarrassment for image classifiers and find it has not healed. Fooling images are classified with near total confidence. Classic attacks were re-run on modern classifiers. The transformer proved most susceptible, with far fewer queries. SPOOF fools networks with minimal pixel changes.

The images stay unrecognizable, at far less compute. Retraining grants only partial resistance; SPOOF adapts and keeps winning. Overconfidence reveals texture learning, not concepts. Deployments carry this fragility until models know their limits. A cheap attack keeps the fragility measurable.
arxiv-2512-06385:
Alessandro Casu and four co authors model how vaccine uptake depends on what people's social circles believe. Their framework, SIS-Vo, couples a classic disease spread model with the spread of opinions on a signed network, where ties can be friendly or hostile. Policy messages do not land the same way on every group, so the model lets each demographic slice answer in its own way.

The authors work out the resting states of the joint system, one with no disease and one where disease persists. They give conditions, in terms of the contact network and how much vaccination each opinion state allows, for the healthy state to hold steady. Simulations then show how well aimed policy messages, working through opinion shifts, can push a population toward the healthy state. The model offers a base for designing vaccine campaigns that stay robust even when false claims target one group.
arxiv-2512-06485:
Kush Revankar and four co authors present Sanvaad, a two way communication aid for deaf users, blind users, and the hearing people around them. Most tools serve one direction only: signs to text, say, but not back. Sanvaad joins both directions in one light framework that runs on ordinary phones and computers without special hardware.

For deaf users, a camera module reads Indian Sign Language from hand landmarks, chosen for its low computing cost. Speech from a phone is turned the other way, into sign clips or letter by letter sign views. For blind users, a screen free voice interface reads, sums up, and speaks text, with speech support in several languages. A simple web interface ties the parts together for desktop and mobile use. The system aims at daily, practical access rather than lab demos.
arxiv-2512-06785:
Vasileios Sevetlidis, George Pavlidis, and Antonios Gasteratos learn a classifier when only some positive examples are labeled and the rest of the data is a mystery mix. This positive unlabeled setting is common: a lab may know some true cases while the bulk of records could be either class. Older methods estimate the risk from negatives they do not have, or guess labels for the rest, and both can collapse in high dimensions.

Their method, AngularPU, works on the unit sphere, where each item is a direction. One learnable prototype direction stands for the positive class, and an item is called positive when its angle to the prototype is small enough. A regularizer pushes the unlabeled items to spread over the sphere instead of crowding near the prototype, which sharpens the split. Theory backs the angle rule. Benchmarks put it at or above the leading rivals.
arxiv-2512-07185:
Jaka Nugraha and co-authors rethink why students actually use e-learning systems, taking aim at a standard adoption model. Universities pour money into platforms, yet engagement lags, and the classic framework says support conditions, things like infrastructure and help, should directly drive the intention to use them. In a survey of several hundred Indonesian university students, that direct link simply was not there. Support conditions showed no significant effect on intention at all.

What the data show instead is an enabling path. Support strongly lifted two other drivers: students' belief that the system improves their performance, and their sense that it is easy to use. Those beliefs, plus social influence and plain enjoyment, did predict intention, and intention predicted real use. Enjoyment was the single strongest driver of intention in the study.
arxiv-2512-07785:
Eli Gendreau-Distler, Joshua Ho, Dongwon Kim, Luc Tomas Le Pottier, Haichen Wang, and Chengxi Yang wrote this 2025 physics computing paper. High energy physics analyses are long chains of code and data steps. The authors test whether language model agents can run such a chain alone.

Their case study is a Higgs boson measurement using ATLAS open data. A hybrid system pairs an agent with the Snakemake workflow manager. Snakemake enforces that every step runs reproducibly and in order. The agent, acting as supervisor and coder, writes the analysis code. It executes the code and repairs its own errors. The team scores success rates, error patterns, costs, and call counts. A spread of leading models, commercial and open-weight, faces the same workflow. Even at zero temperature, final outputs still vary between runs.  The study is the first agent-driven automated analysis framework in the field.
arxiv-2512-07885:
Davide Donno, Donatello Elia, Gabriele Accarino, Marco De Carlo, Enrico Scoccimarro, and Silvio Gualdi wrote this 2025 climate science paper. Tracking tropical cyclones across their lives is vital for weather and climate work. Classic trackers lean on hand-set thresholds that can bias results by region.

Their framework, ByteStorm, rebuilds cyclone tracks with deep learning instead. Detection uses only two fields: vorticity at a mid level and sea-level pressure. Networks classify and localize each cyclone center from those fields alone. A linking algorithm named BYTE then stitches centers into full tracks. The method is benchmarked against top deterministic trackers worldwide. All major formation basins enter the comparison. Detection skill and false alarm rates come out strong in the tests. Seasonal and year-to-year variability are reproduced faithfully by the tracks. The rebuilt paths are smooth and coherent rather than jumpy.  Data-driven tracking is ready beside the classics.
arxiv-2512-08185:
Jinghao Wang, Ping Zhang, and Carter Yagemann, researchers in computing and health, posted a framework proposal on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the security of medical large language models, now used for clinical decision support in many specialties. Testing these models against jailbreaking and privacy attacks is hard for most researchers, since benchmarks demand graphics clusters, paid access, or protected patient data.

Their framework is built to run on an ordinary home computer with freely available models. It covers specialties ranked by clinical risk, from emergency medicine and psychiatry down to general practice. The attacks include role playing, fake authority, and multi turn manipulation, plus attempts to extract private data. All test patients are synthetic, so no ethics board approval is needed. The proposal spells out threat models, data generation, protocols, and scoring rules, giving the community a shared base for comparing defenses.
arxiv-2512-08385:
Marc Rovirola, Julia Odena, Anna Castellvi, and a large team of physicists in Spain posted an experimental study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is orbital currents, flows of orbital angular momentum that could carry information through materials much like spin currents do. Making and detecting such currents coherently is still largely unexplored, and sound waves turn out to be a promising handle.

The team drives chiral surface acoustic waves through bilayers of a light metal under a ferromagnet. Two mechanisms can create orbital currents here: an acoustic orbital Hall effect in the metal, and pumping from the magnet itself. Voltage symmetry analysis separates the two. Strong signals appeared only for chromium and titanium layers, not aluminum or cobalt based stacks, exposing how much material and interface quality matter. Sound driven generation also beat electric generation, pointing to phonon control of orbital magnetism.
arxiv-2512-08685:
Sahar Pourandi and coauthors build and tune a computer model for wet granular materials used in industry. Their method tracks many grains and the forces between them, in the regime where grains are only lightly wet. Liquid bridges between grains create a sticky pull, and liquid can move as bridge volumes change over time.

The team tests two reactor grade plastic powders that differ in grain size, density, and surface form, and so wet in different ways. They link rising liquid content to the shift from dry to wet contact through two key volume parameters. Those values are tuned using the angle formed in a rotating drum test. The tuned model matches flow well for the coarser powder, and for the finer powder at low to moderate wetness. Gaps at high wetness point to limits of grain scaling for sticky systems.
arxiv-2512-09085:
Janet Pauketat and coauthors study how mental models of autonomy and sentience shape human reactions to artificial intelligence. Popular narratives entangle the two ideas: autonomy means self governance, while sentience means the capacity to sense and feel. Agents that act on their own and companions that express emotion may trigger different mental models, with different effects.

The team ran pilot studies and four preregistered vignette experiments, describing a system as autonomous, sentient, both, or neither. Activating a sentience model raised general mind perception and moral consideration more than autonomy did. Autonomy, in turn, raised perceived threat more than sentience did. Sentience also raised perceived autonomy more than the reverse. A combined analysis across studies shows sentience changed reactions more on average. By separating the two mental models, the work allows more precise study of human AI interaction. That precision can guide design of anthropomorphic systems and prompting interfaces.
arxiv-2512-09385:
Uisang Lee and colleagues present BugSweeper, a deep learning system for finding vulnerabilities in Ethereum smart contracts at the level of individual functions. Smart contract bugs can lock or drain real money, so fast and accurate detection matters. Many machine learning detectors still depend on rule-based preprocessing written by security experts, which can throw away context and miss new kinds of flaws.

BugSweeper works end to end from source code. Each Solidity function becomes a graph that merges its syntax tree with control-flow and data-flow information. A two-stage graph neural network first filters noise from these graphs, then reasons at a higher level to spot diverse vulnerabilities. In experiments on real-world contracts, BugSweeper significantly outperformed leading detection methods. The authors argue that removing handcrafted rules makes the approach more robust, automated, and scalable for securing contracts.
arxiv-2512-09485:
Xinye Cao leads a large team building security automation for zero-touch networks, the self-managing networks planned for future mobile systems. Those networks are spread out, open, and highly varied, which expands the attack surface. Such defense means handling the whole security life cycle, from making strategies to testing and updating them, while threats keep changing.

Their framework, SecLoop, uses large language models across that entire lifecycle: generation, orchestration, response, and feedback. On top of it, their SA-GRPO algorithm refines strategies by comparing feedback from many parallel runs of the loop, contrasting groups to learn which strategies work. Extensive real-world experiments on five benchmarks, covering many standard attack processes and more than twenty attack types, showed the system beating existing approaches. The authors plan to release their platform publicly to help advance security automation for next-generation communications.
arxiv-2512-09685:
Zeyu Zhang and Haiying Shen study stragglers, the slow workers that hold up distributed deep learning training, in the clean case of identical graphics processors. Homogeneous clusters are popular for training, but how common stragglers are there, what causes them, and whether existing fixes help had not been measured. Their experiments fill that gap.

They find stragglers remain widespread, caused by imbalanced use of processors and bandwidth. Worse, mitigations that switch from synchronous to asynchronous updates may not improve time-to-accuracy and can create more stragglers through higher resource consumption. Their system, STAR, answers with new synchronization modes that group workers for each update. It adds a heuristic plus a learned method for choosing the best mode, resource reallocation to support it, and placement that avoids overloading processors and bandwidth. In trace-driven tests on AWS, STAR cut time-to-accuracy against systems while keeping synchronous training's final accuracy.
arxiv-2512-09785:
Claire Marie Guimond leads a large team of planetary scientists in a review of water and land on temperate rocky planets. How much of a planet's surface is ocean, and how much is dry land, shapes its climate and its chances for life. The review covers three questions. What physical conditions set the ratio of land to sea? How does that ratio affect climate and biology? And could future telescopes measure the ratio on planets around other stars?

The authors trace how water can be delivered to a growing planet and stored deep in its mantle. They explain how water cycles between the interior and the surface, and how the shape of ocean basins controls how much land stays exposed. They also show that maps built from real observations of Earth suggest future large telescopes could separate water from land on distant rocky planets by their differing brightness.
arxiv-2512-10085:
Miguel Abadi proves large deviation inequalities for sums of positively correlated random variables that arrive in clusters. Classic results, from Bernstein and Hoeffding onward, control how far a sum can stray from its mean, but they assume independence. Very few results handle dependence. Abadi studies positively correlated Bernoulli variables, coin flips that tend to agree, modeling phenomena that appear in clusters within an underlying process. Under a very mild condition, he proves several upper deviation inequalities, bounds on the chance of unusually large sums.

The proofs run through a spectral decomposition of a recursive operator built for the problem. Examples show the bounds at work. Clustered dependence is the rule rather than the exception in real data: failures bunch, infections bunch, extreme weather bunches. Independence based bounds can be far too rosy there. Results like Abadi's give risk math an honest footing for bursty phenomena.
arxiv-2512-10585:
Salvatore Capozziello and co-authors ask a pointed question of the newest cosmology data: does dark energy actually change over time? The DESI survey's second data release has stirred claims that the acceleration of the universe is not driven by a fixed cosmological constant. Their critical review, accepted in Physics of the Dark Universe, weighs the evidence rather than assuming it.

The team ran a full Markov chain analysis across a wide stack of data. DESI distance and Lyman-alpha measurements, compressed microwave background likelihoods, early-universe element abundances, cosmic chronometers, and several supernova collections. They work within a popular two-parameter dark energy model. They also test extensions that free the neutrino mass and the effective number of species. Then they assess how strongly the data really prefer a departure from the standard model. The forty-one page verdict is a careful calibration of the current excitement.
arxiv-2512-11085:
Jean-Marc Azaïs, Federico Dalmao, and Yohann De Castro tackle a statistical problem: judging whether a random field varies differently in different directions, using only one observed snapshot. Their data are excursion sets, the regions where the field rises above some level, seen as a black and white image. The field's mean, spread, and even the threshold are unknown.

Their first method extends a classical contour technique to any dimension by studying the directions of boundary normals. Direction parameters follow from a well behaved optimisation problem built on those normals. Their second contribution is a model free test for evenness in two dimensions whose statistic follows a known distribution when the field is uniform in direction. Simulations show the test is accurate and stronger than rivals. They also apply it to cosmic microwave background data from Planck.
arxiv-2512-11185: Vladimir Yankovskiy examines positional auctions, the bidding systems that rank advertisements or listings by slot, when they are placed in a queue setting. Two classic mechanisms are weighed. One is the Vickrey Clarke Groves rule, which charges bidders based on the harm they impose on others. The other is the generalised second price rule used widely in sponsored search. The study continues the author's earlier work on position auctions for sponsored search in marketplaces, extending the analysis to queues and the properties the two mechanisms show there.
arxiv-2512-11385:
Yuya Yamamoto settles a question about special algebraic curves in characteristic p. He extends a theorem that began with work by Igusa in the nineteen fifties for the simplest case and reached genus two only recently. The curves are hyperelliptic, and the property is superspeciality, a strong and rare condition tied to how the curve's shape interacts with the Frobenius map.

The simultaneous equations that detect superspeciality could a priori have complicated repeated answers. The multiplicity one theorem says they do not. Yamamoto's proof runs through the Lauricella system, a family of hypergeometric functions in many variables whose truncated forms assemble the Cartier Manin matrix that governs the curve. By analysing equalities among partial derivatives of those entries, the result now holds for curves of arbitrary genus.
arxiv-2512-11585:
Juuso Luhtala, Vesa Kuikka, and Kimmo Kaski propose fresh ways to rank the key nodes in a network. Standard scores for closeness and betweenness look only at shortest paths. Degree counts only direct links. Such scores can miss how influence really spreads, with loops and repeat visits.

The new scores come from a spread model that counts all paths, walks, and cycles. One score, in-centrality, grades a node as a target of influence. The other, out-centrality, grades it as a source. Tests on real and test networks show the new betweenness still tracks the old one, yet gives more weight to backup routes when main paths fail.
arxiv-2512-11685:
Niccolò Maffezzoli and co-authors map the ice in every glacier on Earth with a learning model named IceBoost v2.0. Knowing ice thickness is key for sea level forecasts, yet most glaciers have never been probed. The model trained on 7 million thickness measures plus shape and physics clues.

It mapped both recent world glacier lists, over 215,000 and 274,000 glaciers, plus 955 ice bodies by Greenland. Total glacier volume came to about 149 thousand cubic kilometers, give or take 38 thousand. That equals about 323 millimeters of sea level rise. In the high Arctic its errors ran 20 to 45 percent below older methods.
arxiv-2512-11885:
Jackson Stingley builds a bouncing universe model inside Einstein-Cartan gravity, where spin adds torsion to spacetime. In an ekpyrotic model, a steep scalar field drives slow contraction that smooths space. Here the spin fluid grows as the universe shrinks and can halt the crush, causing a bounce with no singularity.

Stingley extends a classic dynamical system to six dimensions, adding shear, curvature, and spin torsion. Numerical runs show the ekpyrotic phase damps shear fast. As contraction deepens, the spin term takes over and triggers the bounce at high but finite density. Maps of the tuning space show a finite island of good bounces. Chaos tests come back quiet in this uniform setup.
arxiv-2512-12085:
Noam Izem and co-authors link two famous puzzles: Anderson localization and the KPZ universality class. In a disordered quantum system, waves can freeze in place instead of spreading, the Anderson effect. Its fluctuations have resisted a unified picture for decades.

Large simulations now show the log density fluctuations of both frozen eigenstates and moving wave packets follow KPZ scaling, the law of growing rough surfaces. Inside the frozen states sits a glassy structure like a directed polymer: dominant paths, pinning, and avalanches. Localization runs along weak branches, not evenly. Wave packet shapes keep a stretched exponential form that still fits single parameter scaling. The KPZ frame gives localization a fresh organizing idea.
arxiv-2512-12285:
Lujuan Dang and Zilai Wang present a neural network that blends physics with fractional calculus to track battery charge in a 2025 paper. Knowing the state of charge of a lithium-ion battery is key for safety and good use. Plain data driven models miss the memory like behavior of the chemistry inside, so their guesses can drift.

Their model, FDIFF-PINN, builds a fractional order circuit model into the network's training rules. Fractional calculus handles processes that depend on their past, which suits battery behavior. They test it on charge and discharge data from Panasonic 18650PF cells. Tests ran at temperatures from -10 to 20 degrees Celsius.
arxiv-2512-12585: Zesen Huang, Marco Velli, and Yuliang Ding offer a model for switchbacks, the sharp kinks in the Sun's magnetic field seen by the Parker Solar Probe. Their solitary Alfven wave model twists open magnetic field lines in three dimensions while keeping the field strength constant. Embedded rotational discontinuities sharply deflect the otherwise uniform field lines, producing localized, large amplitude reversals in one dimensional profiles. Traveling through such curved segments, they argue, is what makes switchbacks appear in spacecraft data.
arxiv-2512-12885:
Minghao Zhu and co-authors present SignRAG, a system that names road signs without training on labeled sign photos. Naming signs matters for smart transport, but the number of sign classes is huge. Building a full labeled set for all of them is not practical.

SignRAG first uses a vision language model to describe a sign in words. That text then pulls a short list of likely matches from a store of reference designs. A large language model picks the final match from that short list. On 303 Ohio regulatory signs, the system scored 95.58 percent on clean images and 82.45 percent on hard real-world road data.
arxiv-2512-12985:
Xiaoshan Huang and co-authors model what happens when a star is torn apart by a black hole, an event called a tidal disruption. Early light comes from both infalling matter and shocks. The debris must settle into a disk before steady feeding can start.

Using three-dimensional radiation simulations, they track disk formation after the debris streams collide with each other. A more rounded disk formed about 24 days after the collision, once the inflow rate passed its peak. Shocks and a lopsided glowing surface drove wide swings in the X-ray to optical light ratio. Their spectra match observed events in broad terms.
arxiv-2512-13185:
Dominik Geissler and Tobias Winkler connect probabilistic programming with automata theory to compute exact inferences. Probabilistic programs look like ordinary code but include random sampling and conditioning. A central task is exact inference: finding the true output distribution for a given input.

Their approach encodes distributions over program variables as weighted automata, a version of finite automata where transitions carry numeric weights. Even distributions with infinite support can be captured this way. The meaning of programs then matches classic automata constructions such as product and concatenation. The work covers a restricted class of discrete probabilistic programs and lays out ongoing research.
arxiv-2512-13385:
Juan Goncalves-Dosantos and co-authors study claims problems with history, bargaining setups where a group must split an endowment too small to cover everyone's claims. Unlike the classic one-shot problem, real disputes repeat over periods, and past settlements may shape fair current ones.

They introduce a historical operator that extends any standard one-shot rule into a rule that accounts for the past. They study which fairness properties survive that extension and give a characterization of the operator itself. The work brings repeated allocation problems, from bankruptcy to resource sharing, into the formal claims framework used by economists.
arxiv-2512-13485:
Andreas Zmija and co-authors report the first measurements of third-order correlation functions of stars with the H.E.S.S. optical intensity interferometer. Third-order correlations give access to closure phase, a quantity that helps reconstruct the shapes of observed objects. No astrophysical third-order signal had been recorded before, since the three-photon signal is extremely faint.

They observed two stellar systems, Nunki and Dschubba, in 2023 and separated the three-photon term from two-photon background. The sensitivity was not yet enough to extract closure phase from the stars. A laboratory test with a pseudo-thermal light source did yield the expected signal, proving the analysis chain works.
arxiv-2512-13685:
Dylan Phelps and co-authors test whether language models detect Alzheimer's disease from meaning, not just surface wording. Alzheimer's is a progressive condition that harms cognition, and speech tasks such as picture description can reveal early signs. A risk is that models learn shallow text patterns instead of true markers of decline.

Their pipeline rewrites texts with new syntax and vocabulary while keeping the meaning fixed. The rewrites score low on word overlap yet high on semantic similarity. Models still classified nearly as well, with only small shifts in macro-F1. Tests that rebuilt images from descriptions added noise and hurt accuracy. The result suggests semantic loss itself is a detectable sign of the disease.
arxiv-2512-13985:
Emilio Fernando Altamirano-Muñiz presents a generalized form of the Least Squares with Virtual Displacements method for soil shear strength. Geotechnical engineers estimate shear strength parameters from triaxial tests on many soil samples. The method seeks a common tangent across many Mohr circles, even when measurement errors make an exact solution impossible.

Beyond the original linear form, he adds logarithmic, parabolic, polynomial, power law, and generalized variants. Those let the method fit the varied failure envelope shapes seen in cohesionless, frictional, and mixed soils. He benchmarks the variants against the p-q method and CTPAC under synthetic noise, comparing robustness and how each method picks representative points. Results highlight the method's flexibility for complex soil behavior.
arxiv-2512-14185:
Emanuele Artioli, Farzad Tashtarian, and Christian Timmerer present ELVIS in a 2025 paper on video streaming. Streaming must balance sharp picture quality with smooth playback, and standard codecs send all the video data because they cannot use scene context.

ELVIS pairs server side encoding gains with client side generative inpainting, which removes redundant data and rebuilds it at the viewer end. Its modular design accepts different codecs, inpainting models, and quality metrics. Results show gains of up to 11 VMAF points over baseline methods, where VMAF is a video quality score. The authors note that heavy compute demands still block real time use, but call the system a first step toward generative streaming.
arxiv-2512-14885:
Patrick Müller and five coauthors map out how to cool and control ions of thulium, a rare earth metal, with laser light. Singly ionized thulium, written Tm+, is a candidate platform for advanced quantum devices. To use it, researchers need a full road map of the light frequencies that cycle the ions and the fine splittings in their energy levels.

Working with ions held in a trap, the team measured the main cycling transition at 313 nanometers and partner lines at 448 and 453 nanometers. They found the near infrared repumping frequencies needed to keep the cycle running, and pinned down hyperfine constants for all key levels. They also studied a long lived metastable state as a possible home for a sturdy qubit, measuring its lifetime and its microwave spectrum with kilohertz precision.
arxiv-2512-15085:
Ehsan Roohi builds AI surrogates that make rare gas flow simulations run in real time. Rarefied flows, where gas is so thin that molecules rarely collide, appear in micro nozzles and high altitude flight. The trusted kinetic solvers, like DSMC, cost so much computing that design work crawls.

Roohi's framework pairs deep neural networks with neural operators. GPU native network surrogates replace costly closure steps in Fokker Planck methods, with big speedups and no loss of accuracy. Physics guided, shock aware DeepONet models handle micro nozzle, micro step, and hypersonic flows across regimes while using little training data. Ensemble methods add uncertainty estimates, and a family of experts design adds robustness across wide Mach and Knudsen ranges. The result is a scalable, physics consistent path to fast surrogate modeling.
arxiv-2512-15185:
Sambhu G Nath and six coauthors track how electron flow changes as a thin film crosses from a topological phase to a trivial one. Their films mix indium into a bismuth antimony telluride compound. Adding indium weakens the spin orbit coupling, and near 7 percent indium the material flips its topological character.

In the cleaner, diffusive regime, the magnetoconductance follows the Hikami-Larkin-Nagaoka formula, and its prefactor tracks the band inversion that marks the flip. Past about 15 percent indium, disorder takes over and transport shifts into variable range hopping. There the magnetoconductance strikingly reverses sign, from negative to positive. The team explains that reversal with an incoherent hopping picture plus wavefunction shrinkage, an orbital effect. Their account unifies topology, spin orbit strength, and disorder in one transport map.
arxiv-2512-15285:
Aleksei Shestov and six coauthors propose a way to grade learned embeddings without any labels. Modern representation learning trains on huge unlabeled corpora, and its embeddings generalize well. Yet judging their quality normally needs labeled downstream tasks, which unsupervised work tries to avoid.

Their metric, called Persistence, comes from persistent homology, a topology tool that tracks shapes across scales. It quantifies the geometric structure and topological richness of an embedding space in a fully unsupervised way. Unlike metrics that assume linear separability or simple covariance, it captures global, multi scale organization. Across diverse domains, Persistence matched downstream performance as well as or better than existing unsupervised metrics. It reached top tier correlations, making it a reliable guide for choosing models and hyperparameters without labels.
arxiv-2512-15385:
Julian Oelhaf and six coauthors stress test machine learning guards for electrical power grids. As renewable and distributed generation spread, fixed protection schemes strain, and learning based fault classification and localization promise faster, adaptive decisions. Deployment, though, hinges on robustness when sensors fail or degrade.

Their unified framework benchmarks models under realistic damage, simulated with high fidelity EMT tools: sensor outages, lower sampling rates, and transient communication losses. Fault classification stayed stable under most damage but fell by about 13 percent under single phase loss. Fault localization proved more fragile, with voltage loss raising its error by over 150 percent. The framework also names which measurement channels are critical for resilient operation. The findings give concrete guidance for building learning based protection that survives bad data.
arxiv-2512-15485:
Eigil Fjeldgren Rischel gives a universal property for measure theoretic probability in a 2025 paper, building on work by Chen. The setting is the Markov category BorelStoch, whose objects are standard Borel spaces and whose maps are Markov kernels, the formal version of random transitions. A universal property pins down such a structure by its relationships alone.

To get there, Rischel introduces coinflips, an unbiased binary choice, inside a Markov category. Such coinflips are unique when they exist and are kept by all Markov functors that preserve coproducts. The paper also gives universal descriptions of several Markov categories of discrete kernels. The results add firm categorical foundations for probability theory.
arxiv-2512-15585:
Yuhang Liu and co authors characterize a compact plastic scintillator sensor that tells apart fast neutrons, thermal neutrons, and gamma rays in a 2025 paper. Sorting these signals in mixed radiation fields matters for reactor work and for cutting background in nuclear experiments. One small sensor that does all three is the goal.

The sensor couples a plastic scintillator, either EJ276 or EJ200, to an EJ426 thermal neutron screen, read by a single photomultiplier tube. Calibrated with cesium, sodium, and cobalt sources, it is tested with an americium beryllium neutron source under varied moderator thickness. The EJ276 version shows three clear signal groups, one for each radiation type.
arxiv-2512-15685:
Oleg Melnikov and co authors present SICAMS, a statistical framework for finding and classifying faults in water distribution networks, in a 2025 paper. Leaks waste water and can grow if missed, yet sensor data from pressure and flow meters are tangled by spatial correlations. Operators need detection that works without a calibrated hydraulic model.

SICAMS whitens the sensor data, then builds a Hotelling T squared statistic as a hypothesis test for normal operation. That statistic tracks total leakage volume, so losses can be estimated by regression. A heuristic sorts events into abrupt leaks, slow leaks, and sensor faults, and sensor rankings give a coarse leak location. Tests on the BattLeDIM L-Town benchmark show high sensitivity, even with several leaks at once.
arxiv-2512-15985:
Sai Karthikey Pentapati, Gregoire Phillips, and Alan Bovik present hierarchical neural surfaces for 3D mesh compression in a 2025 paper. Implicit neural representations compress images, video, and audio well, but most work encodes signed distance functions rather than the triangle meshes that industry actually uses. Bridging that gap is the aim here.

Their method maps a zero genus mesh surface onto a unit sphere, then encodes the displacement field that rebuilds the original shape as a neural representation. A hierarchical design recovers coarse structure first and fine detail later, which keeps the code compact. Meshes of arbitrary resolution can be decoded in real time, with state of the art quality for the compressed size.
arxiv-2512-16185:
Gourab Ghatak proposes a clustering method with a wireless twist in an arXiv paper from 2025. Clustering groups points around centers, and the K-harmonic means variant is less sensitive to bad starting centers than classic K-means. Ghatak adds weights, making a regularized version called weighted K-harmonic means, with soft assignments based on inverse distance.

He proves the method converges under fixed starts, under random starts from a binomial point process, and almost surely under mild decay conditions, the first such stochastic guarantees for harmonic-mean clustering. The weights turn out to match fractional user association by signal strength in wireless networks. Simulations show a better trade-off between weakest signal strength and load fairness than classic and modern rivals. That makes the method a principled tool for placing radio nodes and assigning users.
arxiv-2512-16685:
Gonçalo Gaspar Alves and coauthors test few-shot fingerprinting, a way to spot the same person across medical image sets. When open data sets are merged, the same subject can appear twice, a leak that inflates test scores if training and test data overlap.

Their method maps all scans of one subject to one zone in a learned feature space, so matches can be found by closeness. A ResNet-50 trained with triplet margin loss was tested on 3D MRI and 2D chest X-ray data. Scores stayed high even in hard cases: 90.06 percent recall in 500-way one-shot tests on ChestXray-14, and 98.86 percent in 100-way three-shot tests on BraTS-2021.
arxiv-2512-16785:
M. A. Ortiz-Ferreyro, J. Sumaya-Martinez, and A. Esquivel-Navarrete analyze how light squeezes through holes smaller than its wavelength. The effect is surprising, and is called enhanced transmission. They use a modal frame for the two basic polarizations inside the hole.

Guided modes inside the aperture govern what gets through. How they mix matters too. Tracking the time-averaged Poynting vector, the energy flow map, the team shows a topological switch at resonance. Vortices, saddles, and backflow zones appear. Energy funnels through the hole. Strong phase slopes and phase defects track the excited modes. The same picture covers slits and channels, for perfect conductors and past plasmonic cases.
arxiv-2512-16985:
Marc Riembau and Minho Son build a general frame for energy correlators from spinning sources. An N-point energy correlator maps how energy flux spreads across detectors, but plain versions wash out the spin structure of both source and detector layout.

Their spinning correlators restore that angular data as a series. Unitarity and energy positivity confine the values to a sharply bounded zone, whose edge is reached by pure spin states. First computations cover spinning correlators in QCD and joint energy-charge versions. Because the new measures barely feel soft infrared effects, they probe the hard core of a collision. Extended sum rules for spin and charge close the frame.
arxiv-2512-17085:
Ernő Buzás and Attila Szilva model the charm of independent voters, a flexible minority that can sway polarized elections. Using a modified Deffuant model, where agents shift opinions toward those they meet within a tolerance, they vary how open agents are to switching.

Even simple splits in openness spawn rich outcomes. Open-minded agents can block full convergence into party blocs, give rise to short-lived centrist clusters, or line up with major parties in the end. Small shifts in openness values reshape the whole map of political competition. The patterns mirror real independent voter behavior and offer a simple account of swinging outcomes and unstable centrist coalitions.
arxiv-2512-17185:
Sandeep Neela presents Systemic Risk Radar, a framework that models markets as multi-layer graphs to warn of crashes early. Crises grow from tangled links across sectors, markets, and investor behavior, not from lone price moves, so price-only alarms miss the build-up.

The radar was tested on three crises: the dot-com crash, the Global Financial Crisis, and the COVID-19 shock. Snapshot graph networks, a simple temporal graph prototype, logistic regression, and random forests were compared. Structural network features gave useful early signals past feature-only models. The author proposes richer layers for sector exposure and sentiment, and stronger time models, to cover more crisis types.
arxiv-2512-17685:
Sarvesh Mangla and the MeerKLASS collaboration release the first sky maps from a new way of sweeping the radio sky. South Africa's MeerKAT telescope scanned back and forth over 268 square degrees, recording every two seconds, instead of staring point by point. A new on-the-fly imaging method then stitches those sweeps into clean pictures.

Sixteen hours of scans yielded a catalog of 34,874 radio sources, each caught at high confidence. The maps are quiet and sharp enough to split close sources, and cross-checks against older surveys show brightness accurate within 5 percent. Splitting the band seven ways also gives each source a color, hinting at its physics. The release proves scanning surveys can serve two sciences at once, a model for the coming SKA telescope.
arxiv-2512-17885:
Frederick A. Gent and four coauthors simulate how galaxies build their magnetic fields. Star explosions stir the gas between stars, and that stirring can grow weak seed fields into strong ones. Past simulations made tangled fields far weaker than the ones telescopes see, which left a puzzle.

Running high detail models on graphics cards, the team finds the tangled field stops growing weaker once a key ratio, the magnetic Prandtl number, reaches only a few hundred. Real space has a far larger ratio, so the result should still hold there. The finding gives galaxy scale models a firm value to use for the small scale field.
arxiv-2512-18085:
Gilson V. Soares, Mauricio Reis, and Adelcio C. Oliveira ask how classical a tidy quantum oscillator can look. Their Gamma Model is a non linear oscillator that can be solved on paper, which makes it a clean test bed. They probe it with the Loschmidt Echo, a measure of how a state overlaps with its time reversed self, and with a roughness score drawn from its Wigner portrait.

The echo hints at chaos, yet the model never leaves its orderly, solvable class. On average the overlap falls as the size of the space the state fills grows. Both the echo and the roughness settle into two steady regimes, a split that helps map where quantum order ends.
arxiv-2512-18785:
Renato Panaro, Christian Röver, and Tim Friede fix a consistency trap in medical evidence synthesis. Trials often report treatment effects for subgroups, like younger patients or those with less disability, but pooling those reports can mislead when trials weight subgroups differently. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, presents a Bayesian method, CAMS, that adjusts for each subgroup's contribution within each trial.

The adjustment uses the information fraction, and it makes interaction findings agree whether analysts start from subgroup data or interaction data. The framework handles lopsided subgroup sizes and lets prior knowledge enter when few trials exist. Demonstrated on seven multiple sclerosis trials, CAMS finds a stronger treatment-by-disability interaction, with lower-disability patients gaining more relapse reduction, while the age result stays put. Reliable subgroup answers guide who should get which therapy.
arxiv-2512-19085:
Chun-Qiu Zhao, Xu Cao, and Jian-Ping Dai work out the spin structure of baryon pairs made in electron-positron annihilation. When the pair comes from a single virtual photon, the spin density matrix is fixed without ambiguity in the center-of-mass frame. Their treatment keeps track of two kinds of symmetry breaking at once.

Parity violation and combined charge-parity violation both enter through the photon's coupling to the baryon pair. The finite electron mass is included as a correction to those effects. The compact formulas they derive feed straight into angular patterns of later decays, and into studies of entanglement between hyperon pairs.
arxiv-2512-19485:
Eva Molnárová and three co-authors clear a path for evolutionary therapy in cancers that lack a blood marker to follow. Evolutionary therapy doses treatment to steer a tumor rather than wipe it out, and it steers by measurement. Prostate and ovarian cases lean on serum markers; metastatic lung cancer has none that are reliable, leaving scans.

The standard scan score, RECIST, tracks a few lesions in one dimension against their smallest past size. It was never built for steering and can miss early regrowth. In a virtual patient model, lesion choice and measurement dimension changed detection a lot. Flat measures helped slightly; only full three-dimensional volumes did the job well.
arxiv-2512-19585:
Ignacio Iacobacci, Zhaozhi Qian, Faroq AL-Tam, and Muhammad AL-Qurishi test whether giving a reasoning model more room to think is really the best spend of compute. New thinking models write long chains before answering, and the length of that chain, the thinking budget, is often treated as a simple dial for quality.

The team varies the budget alongside other settings, such as self-consistency voting and self-reflection, inside one balanced comparison that counts cost as well as accuracy. Longer chains alone, they find, are not the smartest buy. Alternative setups reached better answers for the same or less compute. The study is a buyer's guide for reasoning compute.
arxiv-2512-20285:
Gaurav Rudra Malik and co-authors ask how little it takes to stop a quantum spin chain from behaving ergodically. Their platform is the nonintegrable transverse-field Ising model, a standard testbed for chaotic quantum dynamics. They split the chain into two halves whose interaction strengths differ, with no disorder anywhere.

As the coupling ratio moves away from one, the dynamics become constrained. The team documents the crossover with out-of-time-ordered correlators, level-spacing statistics, and the spectral form factor. They also track operator growth in Krylov space and entanglement in the eigenstates. The results show that one macroscopic inhomogeneity gives a clean, disorder-free route to broken ergodicity in this model.
arxiv-2512-20585:
Nicholas J Ossi, Barbara Prinari, and Jianke Yang rebuild the perturbation theory of dark solitons on solid ground. Dark solitons are dips travelling through a bright background in the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Predicting how small kicks slowly change a soliton's parameters, and what radiation shelves form beside it, needs the right eigenfunction machinery.

Earlier treatments stumbled on blow-up points in the scattering data at branch points of the continuous spectrum. The authors prove closure of the squared functions and assemble the complete set, discrete modes included. From the one-soliton closure relation they derive the slow-time evolution of the soliton's settings and its phase. A pole in the correction integral explains the shelves. Direct computer runs confirm every prediction.
arxiv-2512-20685:
Jonas Arruda and co-authors review, in tutorial form, how diffusion models can serve simulation-based inference. In many fields, a model can be run to produce data for any chosen settings, yet no formula gives the chance of real data. Inference based on simulation turns the model runs into odds over the unknown settings. Diffusion models have lately become strong engines for this job, since they can learn rich shapes over settings and data alike.

The review sorts out the choices in training, use, and testing such models. It covers guidance, score mixing, flow matching, consistency models, and joint models, and shows how noise schedules and samplers trade speed against accuracy. Case studies range over problem sizes, budgets for model runs, and model types. Open questions end the tour, marking where this young field still needs work.
arxiv-2512-20785:
Mikhail Lazarev and Andrey Ustyuzhanin ask whether formulas, not just predictions, can be learned from materials data. Neural networks predict well but hide their reasoning inside millions of numbers. Symbolic regression instead searches for a readable equation that fits the data, so scientists can inspect and reuse what the model found.

The authors apply a deep symbolic regression method called SEGVAE to two-dimensional materials with defects. Its results matched or equaled those of leading graph neural network methods on the same properties. Because the output is an equation, it can transfer to new data more sensibly. The authors also weigh where such methods fit across the natural sciences.
arxiv-2512-20985:
Salman Jan, Hassan Ali Razzaqi, Ali Akarma, and Mohammad Riyaz Belgaum put a watchdog ledger underneath autonomous AI agents. Agents that perceive, reason, and act in healthcare, smart cities, forensics, and supply chains are flexible, but their decisions are hard to audit after the fact. The architecture pairs a LangChain-based multi-agent system with a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric blockchain. That chain checks inputs, evaluates proposed actions against policy, and records outcomes immutably.

Trials in smart inventory management, traffic-signal control, and healthcare monitoring show the verification layer blocks unauthorized actions, keeps the whole decision path traceable, and holds latency within workable bounds. For organizations that want agent autonomy in high-impact settings, the design offers a governance pattern where every action can be replayed and justified.
arxiv-2512-21185:
Tanghui Jia, Li Yuan, and twelve co-authors present UltraShape 1.0, a diffusion framework that generates three-dimensional shapes in two passes: a coarse global structure first, then a refinement stage that carves in the detail. A serious data pipeline underpins it. A new watertight processing method and strict filtering repair public 3D datasets. They remove poor samples, fill holes, and thicken fragile walls while keeping fine features intact.

Refinement works voxel by voxel at fixed positions. Queries taken from the coarse shape act as positional anchors. They are encoded so the diffusion model can devote itself to local surface detail inside a smaller, structured search space. It no longer has to juggle location and detail at once. Trained only on public data with modest resources, the system matches strong open-source rivals in geometry quality, and the team promises full release of code and models.
arxiv-2512-21585:
Lijun Bo, Dongfang Yang, and Shihua Wang model how data products should be priced over time in a demand-driven market. Their game has three tiers: a single data buyer at the top, an intermediary broker in the middle, and a group of competing sellers at the bottom. Each side acts strategically, anticipating the others' moves.

Data quality evolves dynamically, and the sellers' quality investments interact through mean field effects, captured by coupled stochastic differential equations. For fixed pricing policies, the authors derive the sellers' approximate Nash equilibrium strategies with mean field game methods. The broker's best pricing rule comes from solving its Stackelberg leadership problem. The buyer's procurement policy follows from an optimal control problem involving conditional mean field forward-backward equations. Under regularity conditions, the three strategies together form an approximate Stackelberg equilibrium. The framework gives market designers a tractable way to reason about data marketplaces.
arxiv-2512-21985:
Small vision models deployed in high-stakes settings often rely on spurious correlations. Their explanations expose the mismatch with expert knowledge. Alexander Koebler, Lukas Kuhn, Ingo Thon, and Florian Buettner introduce LVLM-VA, a method that uses a large vision-language model to align a small task-specific model's behavior with human domain knowledge.

The framework is a bidirectional interface: it translates model behavior into natural language for experts, and maps human class-level specifications back into image-level critiques of the model. On synthetic and real-world datasets, the alignment substantially reduced reliance on spurious features and group-specific biases. It did so without needing fine-grained feedback. The appeal is efficiency: the big model's generalization is spent on guidance, while the deployed model stays small and explainable.
arxiv-2512-22585:
Andrea Giorgini, Jingning He, and Hao Wu analyze a mathematical model of two mixed fluids whose densities differ, coupled to a dissolved chemical that attracts motion. The model blends Navier-Stokes flow with a Cahn-Hilliard description of the fluid interface, and it is built from Onsager's variational principle so that energy and dissipation stay thermodynamically consistent. Chemotaxis and mass transport inside the mixture are both included.

For the two-dimensional problem with boundary conditions, the authors prove that global finite-energy and weak solutions always exist, using approximations and compactness arguments. With smoother starting data they prove a unique strong solution exists and that weak solutions gain regularity over time. One notable result: the chemical's density stays bounded forever when it starts bounded, because diffusion driven by chemical potential blocks the blow-up seen in the classical Keller-Segel system.
arxiv-2512-22685:
Ramiro de la Reza and four co-authors study lithium-rich giant stars in the Galaxy's oldest neighborhoods, where the phenomenon is barely explored. The authors work from two large LAMOST catalogues of low-mass field giants. The stars are both lithium-rich and lithium-poor, with metallicities down to a ten-thousandth of the Sun's. They trace lithium enrichment across the halo and thick disc. The stages covered run from red giant branch through horizontal branch and asymptotic giant branch.

Many enriched giants show infrared excesses, evidence of recent mass loss and of the Cameron-Fowler mechanism minting fresh lithium-7 in episodes. The authors set new lithium-richness thresholds for each evolutionary stage. Rotation tells its own story: above a plateau near forty kilometers per second, richer stars spin faster at lower metallicity, implying stellar models need longer-lived helium-3 reservoirs.
arxiv-2512-23285: Persi Diaconis, Andrew Lin, and Arun Ram diagonalize a slow-mixing Markov chain on binary strings. The chain wanders over all strings of a fixed length and takes a long time to forget its starting point, so sharp convergence rates matter. The authors bring in the machinery of algebraic combinatorics: representation theory, Murphy elements, and above all Schur-Weyl duality. That duality relates the symmetries of permuting coordinates to those of rotating the space. From it they construct an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions, which delivers sharp convergence rates.
arxiv-2512-23385:
The Anh Nguyen, Triet Huynh Minh Le, and M. Ali Babar mine developer discussions to chart real security problems of AI projects. AI builders face ordinary software supply chain risks plus novel threats against models and data, yet little was known about which issues practitioners hit and how they fix them. The authors gathered discussions from Hugging Face and GitHub, filtering them with a pipeline that pairs keyword matching with a fine-tuned classifier chosen after comparing models.

The pipeline produced a dataset of more than three hundred thousand security discussions. A thematic analysis of a sample yielded thirty-two security issues and twenty-four solutions across software, external tools, models, and data. Many problems trace to tangled dependencies and black-box AI components. Model and data issues often lacked solutions. The authors offer the taxonomy as evidence-based guidance for securing links of the AI supply chain.
arxiv-2512-23585:
Dat Le, Thomas Manhardt, Moritz Venator, and Johannes Betz look for rare and dangerous driving situations in naturalistic driving data, the kind of edge cases autonomous vehicles must handle safely. Because such scenarios are by definition uncommon, labeling enough of them by hand is impractical, so the team turned to unsupervised anomaly detection that needs no labeled examples.

Their framework uses Deep Isolation Forest, which pairs neural network features with isolation forests to flag complex anomalies. Data from perception modules, describing vehicle dynamics and surroundings, were converted into statistical features over sliding time windows, with a t-SNE projection helping humans inspect what was flagged. Judged against proxy ground truth and by watching the flagged video frames. The approach reliably surfaced rare, hazardous scenarios, though the authors note their hand-built features cannot capture every real-world anomaly. The team checked each flagged clip by eye.
arxiv-2512-23685:
Quancheng Liu and Klaus Ziegler find a measurable handle on the topology of two-band materials. In such systems, each energy band's eigenfunctions define a Bloch vector field over momentum space. How many times that field winds around is a topological invariant: an integer that cannot change under smooth deformations of the material's Hamiltonian. Winding numbers are usually computed, not measured directly.

The authors show the Bloch vector can be reconstructed from the gradient of the energy dispersion, the slope of the band. Since that slope is proportional to the electrons' group velocity, and band dispersions are exactly what angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy records, topology becomes accessible to experiment. Their mapping between the dispersion gradient and the Bloch vector gives a direct, measurable relation between a two-band Hamiltonian and its topological structure. In short, a band map can now serve as a map of the field's twist.
arxiv-2512-23785:
Sahan Sanjaya, Aruna Jayasena, and Prabhat Mishra survey power side-channel attacks, in which secrets leak through a device's electricity use. Every computation draws data-dependent power, and careful measurement of consumption, or of related signals such as stray radio waves, heat, sound, and timing, can expose what a system is doing. Existing surveys concentrate on attacks against cryptographic code.

This survey ranges wider, classifying recent attacks and countermeasures by application domain. Beyond key extraction from cryptographic code, power analysis has been used to reverse-engineer machine learning models, exploit data about user behavior. It can even pull apart a processor's instructions one by one from its power trace. For each domain the authors compare attacks on application-specific terms and collect the defenses proposed against them. The result is a map of where power leakage threatens systems that never handle classical encryption keys.
arxiv-2512-24885:
Hengli Li, Zhaoxin Yu, Qi Shen, and others formalize how beliefs should guide strategic dialogue acts such as adversarial and alignment moves. Earlier systems estimated beliefs about an opponent or partner accurately but had no principled way to use those beliefs while generating replies. Their approach, BEDA, turns beliefs into probabilistic constraints on what an agent may say.

A world set, a belief estimator, and a conditional generator select an act and produce utterances consistent with the constraints. Dialogue researchers get a process linking estimation to action. Strategic conversation, from negotiation to debate, needs exactly that bridge between reading a partner and choosing words.
arxiv-2601-06785:
Research by Tadashi Arimitsu and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with conformal preimage decay exponent of the julia sets of rational graph-directed markov systems. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. We define and investigate the conformal preimage decay exponent of the Julia sets of rational graph-directed Markov systems.

The authors show that this exponent coincides with the difference between the topological entropy and upper sequential capacity topological pressure. For the rational skew product map associated with the system S S. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-06885:
