Grit scores showed no significant correlation with academic success. The conversations nonetheless split the groups sharply in approach. High-grit students studied deeper, directed themselves, and weathered pressure calmly. Low-grit peers chased assessments more narrowly. Bhatia still calls grit worth cultivating in trainees.
pmc-13241585:
Liamvilairat and colleagues at Mahidol University fed perilla seed oil to mice with smoke-induced lung damage resembling COPD. The oil is rich in alpha-linolenic acid and known for antioxidant effects. Mice received a lower or higher daily dose by gavage for two or four weeks. Lung injury came from weekly injections of cigarette smoke extract.

Smoke exposure enlarged airspaces and flooded lung wash fluid with inflammatory cells. Oil treatment, especially the short course at the lower dose, shrank the airspace enlargement. Eosinophil counts fell under both treatment lengths. Longer dosing also cut a blood marker of lipid oxidation, supporting a protective dietary role.
pmc-13242485:
Murat Erem and colleagues compared screw and plate layouts for fixing steep femoral neck fractures in the laboratory. Their study appeared in the Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery in 2026. Pauwels type III fractures face strong vertical shear, and the standard medial buttress plate demands deep dissection. The team built the fracture in twenty-five synthetic thigh bones and tested five fixation combinations under a loading machine.

An inverted triangle of screws paired with an anteromedial support plate carried the highest load before failure. An L-shaped screw layout with the same front plate performed worst, possibly because the plate created a stress riser. Group differences did not reach statistical significance, though the spread between best and worst was large. Most bones finally broke below the implants. The authors say the front plate matches the buttress plate's stability while offering a safer surgical route.
pmc-13243885:
Linh Van Nguyen and co-authors captured the first detailed footage of burrow life in the Annamite striped rabbit, one of the world's least known mammals. Their study appeared in Ecology and Evolution in 2026. Six camera traps watched suspected burrows in wet evergreen forest in the Annamite Mountains between May and October 2024. Sites were chosen through interviews with local people and field surveys across a band of hillside elevations.

Over 864 trap nights the cameras recorded 1,293 videos of the endangered rabbit. The footage shows a full routine of opening, closing, and hiding the burrow mouth, packing soil and small stones over the entrance. One continuous event lasting over three hours looks like a birth in progress. Forty-six days later the female left the burrow flanked by two juveniles, the first such record for the species. The authors say burrow secrecy may be central to how this rabbit survives.
pmc-13245785:
Harper and Boehme tested whether brief oxygen shortage can armor the eye against blast injury, in this 2026 PLOS One study. Retinal ganglion cells, which carry visual signals to the brain, are sensitive to blast-wave brain injury and die progressively afterward. Mice received six sessions of low-oxygen preconditioning over two weeks before a shock-tube blast, and their retinal function and structure were measured four weeks later.

Blast-exposed mice without preconditioning showed weaker retinal electrical responses and thinner nerve layers, with fewer surviving ganglion cells counted under the microscope. Preconditioned blast mice were statistically indistinguishable from uninjured controls on those measures. The authors conclude that repeated hypoxic preconditioning gives at least partial protection, a lead for shielding soldiers and others at blast risk, though far from clinical use.
pmc-13247285:
Ashfaq, Mariyam, and Aziz hunted for typhoid drug candidates inside existing medicines in this 2026 Bioinformatics and Biology Insights study. Typhoid Salmonella increasingly resists antibiotics, so the team targeted DHQ1, a bacterial enzyme in the shikimate pathway that humans lack, which bacteria need to build essential amino acids. They screened five hundred fifty-one compounds in the computer against the enzyme's structure.

Docking simulations plus drug-likeness and safety filters narrowed the field to ten strong binders, including the HIV drug cabotegravir, the plant compound limonin, and the milk-thistle extract silibinin. Molecular dynamics simulations checked that the best candidates stayed gripped to the enzyme. The authors present these repurposed, already de-risked drugs as starting points for laboratory testing against drug-resistant typhoid.
pmc-13247985:
Matthews and co-authors measured whether a student-run telehealth coaching clinic actually improves clients' lives, in this 2026 International Journal of Telemedicine and Applications study. Student-led clinics give trainees experience while serving underserved communities, but their patient outcomes are rarely reported. The Australian team collected before-and-after quality-of-life scores from three hundred sixty-nine coaching participants between 2020 and 2024, converting them to standard utility values.

Average utility rose significantly after participation. Gains were largest in participants who started worst off, followed by younger adults and women, and spread across physical, psychological, and environmental domains. The authors present the clinic as a promising, low-cost part of the healthcare ecosystem and, unusually for this literature, attach outcome numbers rather than satisfaction quotes alone.
pmc-13249185: Mirsalehi and colleagues published this correction in PLOS One in 2026. It amends their paper on using convolutional neural networks to predict an ectasia screening index for keratoconus from raw Casia2 scanner data. Three values in Table 4 were printed incorrectly: the accuracy and sensitivity reported for the adapted ResNet 18 model, and the F1 score for the adapted EfficientNetB0 model. The notice points readers to the corrected table in the updated article. The study's overall approach and conclusions are not withdrawn.
pmc-13249685:
McGetrick and colleagues tested pupil readings as an early warning in children on life support, in a 2026 European Journal of Pediatrics study. Seventy-five children received ECMO, a machine that takes over heart and lung work, and brain injury is a leading danger in such care. A handheld device scored pupil reactivity automatically during the first three days, producing a neurological pupil index.

Thirty-five percent of the children died in hospital. Any reading below the normal threshold in the first seventy-two hours was independently tied to that mortality risk. The link to disability at discharge was weaker and less consistent. The authors present the bedside measurement as a useful early prognostic tool, while calling the disability question open.
pmc-13250285:
Fengyuan Song and colleagues built a skin patch for constipated children in this 2026 study. A traditional Chinese formula called YiNianJin speeds the gut, but swallowing it lets a mercury-based ingredient build up in the body and wastes much of the dose.

The patch carries the formula's active parts in tiny bubbles set into a gel backing, releasing them slowly through the skin. In tests it raised the gut's push rate by about 24 percent and adjusted proteins that control water and mucus in the bowel wall. It also boosted helpful gut signals and friendly bacteria products. The authors see it as a safer way to give complex formulas.
pmc-13250385:
Norouzkhani and colleagues test a game-like phone app for people living with inflammatory bowel disease. Their 2026 Health Science Reports trial ran for twenty-four weeks at several centers, comparing the My IBD Buddy platform with standard care. The app tracked symptoms, supported medication routines, and taught self-management through game elements.

By twelve weeks, app users showed better confidence in managing their disease and stronger disease knowledge than controls. Quality-of-life scores had improved, but not yet by a clearly significant margin at that stage. By week twenty-four, every main outcome favored the app group, and almost all users stayed with the program. The authors recommend gamified telehealth as a scalable addition to routine bowel disease care.
pmc-13251085:
Ayşe Denizkara and colleagues test natural coatings for fish freshness in this 2026 food study. Rainbow trout fillets spoil fast in storage, so the team coated them in beeswax films, some enriched with thyme or laurel essential oils.

Over storage they tracked acidity, spoilage chemicals, texture, colour, and fat makeup. All samples changed over time, but the oil-enriched coatings slowed spoilage, with stronger effects at higher oil levels. Fillets with four percent laurel oil ended with the lowest spoilage readings and the best texture. Thyme coatings kept the most of one healthy fat type, laurel the most of another. The coatings improved freshness and food value overall.
pmc-13251285:
Eide and colleagues test whether imaging tracers injected into spinal fluid can measure how fast the human brain clears fluid. Their 2026 Fluids and Barriers of the CNS study uses two contrast agents, one read by CT and one by MRI. Brain waste clearance through glymphatic and lymph pathways is suspected in degeneration diseases but hard to measure in people.

Fifty-two people received the CT tracer and forty-five the MRI tracer, with scans up to a day after injection. Clearance speeds varied widely between individuals for both agents, and the two measures correlated with each other. Tracer spread through the fluid spaces tracked clearance, most strongly for the MRI agent. The authors say individualized clearance checks are feasible and could refine drug delivery into the spinal fluid.
pmc-13252885:
Caroline Lamarre and colleagues map digital mental health help inside skin care in this 2026 scoping review. Long-term skin diseases such as psoriasis carry heavy rates of depression and anxiety, yet mental health support inside dermatology stays rare.

Searching five databases to March 2025, the team found just eleven studies that paired a digital tool with therapy or psychiatric care for skin patients. Most targeted psoriasis and used internet-based talking therapy or apps that patients worked through alone. Dropout ranged widely, from ten to 76 percent. Six studies reported better skin-related quality of life, and several found real drops in depression and anxiety. The field is small but promising, the authors conclude.
pmc-13252985:
Kacey Lynch and colleagues co-design a social media programme for new mothers' mental health in this 2026 Australian study. Depression and anxiety around childbirth affect up to one in five women, and rural and remote mothers face isolation, staff shortages, and cost barriers to help.

The team ran group talks and interviews with 26 mothers and eight professionals in northern Queensland, advised by a community group. Five core needs emerged: connection and support, respectful personal care, empowering information, place-based and culturally safe help, and low-effort digital formats. Mothers saw social media as a plausible channel for peer connection. The study frames how platform features could meet, or fail, each need.
pmc-13253585:
Sarah Yvonnet and Karin Tybjerg trace how two hard-to-classify diseases swapped strategies in this 2026 history and philosophy article. Classifying sickness always spotlights some features and buries others, and cancer and diabetes, both sprawling and chronic, strained every scheme tried on them.

Historically, cancer was sorted by anatomy and tissue form because its workings stayed opaque, while diabetes, which could not be pinned to one organ, was sorted by body function. Molecular markers now let both diseases be re-sorted along the other disease's favoured lines, so their paths cross. That reopening brings fresh chances and fresh costs, which the authors weigh combining historical and philosophical tools.
pmc-13253885:
Zechun Peng and colleagues test allicin, a compound from garlic, against kidney stones in a 2026 study. Kidney stones are common and often return. The team combined computer-based target hunting, cell tests on harmed kidney cells, and a rat model where stones were induced with a chemical.

Computer screening found 46 shared targets between allicin and stone disease, with TNF as the central one. In cells, allicin raised survival and cut inflammatory factors. In rats, it reduced kidney damage and calcium oxalate deposits. The authors say it works by blocking the TNF/NF-κB pathway, a chain of signals that drives swelling.
pmc-13253985:
Heba Amer and colleagues report a rare pairing of tumor and blood failure in a 2026 case report. A 52-year-old man had a thymoma, a tumor of the thymus gland, left untreated for nine years. He then developed pure red cell aplasia, where the marrow stops making red blood cells while other blood lines stay intact.

Scans showed a large chest mass measuring 16 centimeters. After transfusions, surgeons removed the thymus, and tests confirmed a mixed spindle cell thymoma. His blood fully recovered with no extra immune drugs. The authors call this the first such case reported from Syria.
pmc-13256485:
Junyu Zhao leads a 2026 cross-sectional survey of digital literacy among nursing teachers in Fujian province, China. A cross-sectional survey measures a group at one point in time. The team surveyed 339 teachers from three medical universities and five colleges between July 2023 and June 2024. Their questionnaire was built on a model that adds artificial intelligence to older ideas about teaching with technology.

Overall scores sat at a medium level, with a mean of 101.92. Teachers scored highest on digital awareness and lowest on digital technology knowledge and skills. Older age predicted lower scores in several areas, while teaching experience helped digital application but lowered the technology knowledge score. The authors suggest targeted training for senior staff, more digital resources, and stronger ethics and safety training.
pmc-13256785:
Sitnikova and co-authors review how computer vision might predict which breast cancer patients will respond fully to chemo given before surgery. Response to neoadjuvant therapy varies widely, and doctors cannot yet forecast it well. The review covers machine learning studies on stained whole-slide images of tumor tissue.

Patterns favoring resistance included sparse tumor cells in cord-like groupings, dead tissue, collagen-rich stroma, and heavy blood vessel growth. Sensitivity tracked with dense tumor growth, intense nuclear staining, and many infiltrating lymphocytes. The authors argue that combining image data with other data types should sharpen forecasts. They call for clear, cross-modal tools that also teach biologists about treatment response.
pmc-13259585:
Guillermo Roa Alvarez leads a 2026 case report of bullous pemphigoid linked to a diabetes drug in an elderly woman. Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering skin disease, most common in older adults. The patient was an 81-year-old woman with long-standing type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and linagliptin. Linagliptin belongs to a drug class called DPP-4 inhibitors, which has been tied to this skin disease in earlier reports.

She developed a widespread itchy blistering rash, with tense blisters, erosions, and crusted plaques on her trunk, limbs, and skin folds. Skin biopsy showed a blister under the surface layer with many eosinophils, a type of white blood cell. Fluorescence tests confirmed the diagnosis, and timing pointed to linagliptin with no other trigger found. Stopping the drug and starting prednisone led to steady improvement and no new blisters.
pmc-13259885:
Maleeha Butt and colleagues report a 2026 service project on psychological needs in an ECMO service in north-west England. ECMO, short for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, is a machine that does the work of the heart and lungs for critically ill patients. National guidance says intensive care patients should have access to psychologists, but the team's cardiothoracic unit had none. They measured former patients' mental health, interviewed them, and piloted a six-week ECMO-specific group.

Six weeks after discharge, fifty percent of patients scored in the clinically significant range for anxiety and thirty-seven percent for depression. Patients described feeling powerless and alone, and wondering what is normal after ECMO. The pilot group was well received, with patients saying they felt seen and heard. Anxiety symptoms fell by sixty-six percent and depression symptoms by seventy-eight percent in the small group.
pmc-13260085:
Stella Sandford wrote a 2026 history and philosophy article on Buffon's general theory of reproduction. Buffon was an eighteenth-century French naturalist whose Natural History was a landmark work. Sandford examines his discussion of how animals and plants compare, and his claim that nourishment, development, and reproduction all flow from one general cause. Buffon seems to say both that the animal-plant distinction is absolute and that it is false, and the article explains that puzzle.

Sandford argues the distinction holds for Buffon's first task, classifying nature and describing particular species. It largely drops away in his second task, studying the general processes of life shared by both kingdoms. On her reading, Buffon's theory rests on a vegetal model: reproduction in general works like vegetative multiplication, where a new whole grows from a part.
pmc-13260785:
Bhavana Singh leads a 2026 study of what drives patient satisfaction at a public university hospital in Ghana. Data came from 366 clinic patients surveyed between November 1 and December 20, 2025, using a structured survey. It covered service quality areas from the SERVQUAL model, such as steady service and empathy, plus how well staff communicate. A method for testing linked causes examined how these factors shaped satisfaction, and whether communication carried the effect of service quality.

Median satisfaction and communication scores were both 75.0 on the scales used. The physical side of service was rated highest, while steadiness was rated lowest. Communication, with a coefficient of 0.400, and empathy, at 0.434, were strong drivers of satisfaction. Communication did not carry the link between service quality areas and satisfaction. The authors urge putting patient-first communication and kind care first in quality work.
pmc-13261085:
Sounira Mehri and Josef Finsterer write a 2026 letter on a mitochondrial gene variant and its wide effects. The variant, m.3243A>G in the MT-TL1 gene, affects the cell's energy-making DNA. Carriers can develop diabetes, kidney failure, hearing loss, and heart muscle disease.

The letter discusses a reported 37-year-old woman whose illness included type 2 diabetes, kidney insufficiency, and hearing loss. She also had postpartum heart failure, brainstem atrophy, recurrent miscarriages, and placenta accreta. Her preterm infant, born at 29 weeks, recovered fully after an 81-day hospital stay. The authors argue the mitochondrial disorder could have been suspected earlier from her combined history. They note that the share of mutated DNA, called heteroplasmy, was not reported in affected tissues. That measurement matters for diagnosis and genetic counseling.
pmc-13261985:
Soo Ah Jin, Qi Fang, and Karunakar Sukuru ask whether making softgel capsules or breaking them down shatters a seaweed gum into a suspect fragment. Carrageenan gives plant-based softgels their shell, but its degraded cousin poligeenan carries a toxic name. Their 2026 study stresses this stuff under factory and stomach conditions.

Heat alone, even past boiling point, barely dented them. Lab-made stomach acid nibbled them, yet fragments stayed safely above the danger size. Only acid plus extreme heat tore carrageenan into small pieces. No poligeenan showed up under any real-world condition, supporting carrageenan's continued use in capsules and supplements.
pmc-13262585:
Kunyuan Jiang and colleagues challenge the assumption that giant liver tumors fare worse after surgery than merely large ones. Their 2026 dual-center study covers two hundred eighty-one patients whose single hepatocellular carcinoma measured at least five centimeters. All underwent curative-intent removal with clean margins.

Giant tumors, ten centimeters and up, arrived with more warning signs, including bigger operations and more transfusions. After matching eighty-two patients per group on those differences, recurrence-free survival came out statistically indistinguishable. Neither group reached median overall survival during follow-up. Blood marker levels and vessel invasion, not sheer size, decided prognosis, the authors conclude.
pmc-13263185:
Charuta Joshi comments on a study of stress in parents of children with epilepsy in a 2026 journal commentary. The study covered 117 children and 149 caregivers, grading children's thinking skills and behavior and parents' stress with standard scales. Joshi frames the findings against the World Health Organization global action plan for epilepsy and brain disorders, which backs family-centered care.

Parents of children with moderate intellectual disability reported higher stress than parents of children with normal cognition. Behavior problems, especially inward-turned ones like anxiety, tracked strongly with stress. Drug-resistant epilepsy and multi-drug treatment added strain. Parents may also under-report stress, the study warned. Joshi and the authors urge routine caregiver screening inside epilepsy care.
pmc-13263285:
Charlotte Proverbs and Daniel Brown present an automatic sunspot tracking program in a 2026 journal article. Sunspots are dark patches on the Sun whose rotation twists the overlying magnetic field, storing energy that can erupt as flares. Measuring that rotation for many sunspots needs automation. Their program, SSTrack, finds and follows sunspots in high-cadence images.

Tested on a four-month sample previously studied with a semi-automatic tool, SSTrack found 54 of the 56 known sunspots, plus 43 more the older method missed. It often spotted sunspots earlier and tracked them longer. Rotation estimates agreed well where the two methods overlapped. The older tool over-read rotation when a sunspot split, because its center estimate shifted with the changing shape.
pmc-13264585:
Katherine E Pelch and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary arguing that PFAS, a group of long-lasting industrial chemicals, can harm the ability to breastfeed, and that this harm is being ignored. They review human and animal evidence on these chemicals and the mammary gland, the tissue that makes milk.

Across varied human groups, mothers with the highest PFAS levels in pregnancy breastfed for shorter times. Animal studies show the mammary gland is among the tissues most sensitive to these chemicals. Yet the authors say a recent United States drinking water safety review and clinical guidance barely used this evidence. They urge that milk-making effects count in future risk reviews, rules, and advice to new mothers.
pmc-13264685:
Ngo Cheung wrote a 2026 synthesis paper linking gene studies of substance use disorders and anxiety under one frame. It draws on five of the author's own early gene studies, which used predicted gene activity rather than direct measures in patients. The paper is openly framed as idea-building, not settled proof.

Cheung sorts the biology into a pruning, plasticity, and aging axis. Early opioid exposure and lighter alcohol patterns tied to immune pruning of brain connections. Heavier dependence tied more to plasticity in reward circuits, energy sensing, and cell power strain. Anxiety leaned toward inflammation, cell death signals, and axon stress. The paper lists tests needed next, including fine mapping and cell-level checks, before the frame can be trusted.
pmc-13264985:
Tingting Yu and colleagues present a 2026 brain imaging study of people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes who are also overweight or obese. Extra weight worsens metabolic harm in diabetes, and early brain changes were little studied. The team mapped how brain regions connect as a network and related the pattern to thinking tests.

They scanned 32 patients and 27 healthy controls at rest. Both groups' networks kept an efficient small-world layout, but the patient group scored lower on that layout and on global efficiency, and signals had to travel longer paths. Local node differences appeared in exploratory checks, including one region whose connectivity rose with body mass. No single abnormal connection survived strict testing. The authors say network damage may start early in this group.
pmc-13268185:
Prateek Chandra Bhan and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial on whether timing matters for aspiration-raising help. Role models can lift people's ambitions, but the effect may fade fast. The team tested a video-based role-modeling session among postgraduate students at a UK university during the Covid-19 pandemic, comparing it with a control group.

Aspirations rose right after the video. Self-reported effort rose later, after a delay. But both gains faded away within a few weeks. The authors describe the evidence as suggestive rather than firm. Their lesson for program designers is practical: when the boost is delivered matters, and one-off sessions likely need reinforcement to last. The paper adds a caution to the optimism around cheap, light-touch motivation programs.
pmc-13269985:
Kevin H McLaughlin and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 sorting older surgical patients into subgroups from routine hospital data. Records covered 2,036 adults aged 65 and over admitted after surgery at one institution. A statistical grouping method used frailty, mobility, daily activity ability, and general health.

Three groups emerged: low frailty with high mobility at 15.3 percent, high frailty with low mobility at 27.6 percent, and low frailty with low mobility at 57.1 percent. Home discharge was highest in the first group at 99 percent and lowest in the frail group at 77 percent. Long stays peaked in the frail group at 27 percent. Therapy visits also ran highest there. The authors suggest tailoring care by group.
pmc-13271385:
Vikas N. O'Reilly-Shah is lead author of a 2026 theoretical article examining the unfolding argument in the neuroscience of consciousness. That argument claims causal structure cannot explain consciousness because any looping neural network can be unfolded into a one-way network with identical behaviour, making the loop irrelevant.

The authors test a boundary case: networks whose connections change quickly through plasticity, the brain's ability to rewire with experience. Through mathematical proofs covering history dependence, stability, and information measures, they show such plastic systems cannot be matched by a static one-way network. Their results do not prove plasticity is needed for consciousness, they stress, but they restore the question as one science can test.
pmc-13271885:
Leonie Hodel is lead author of a 2026 journal article mapping cattle densities across the Brazilian Amazon from very high-resolution satellite images. Cattle ranching is the main driver of deforestation in the world's largest tropical forest, yet herd numbers usually come from coarse census data, hiding fine-scale land use.

A deep learning method counted individual animals in imagery covering over 12,000 square kilometres across four states, combined with pasture maps to estimate stocking rates per property. The conservative estimate was 0.73 head per hectare in 2018-2019, a pattern of extensive land use. Stocking was lower on properties with more recent deforestation and on those farther from slaughterhouses. The authors note coverage and detection limits.
pmc-13272185:
Mitchell R. Koss is lead author of a 2026 retrospective study on delays in surgically fixing distal radius fractures, breaks near the wrist end of the forearm bone. Fixation delayed beyond two weeks is linked to worse patient-reported outcomes, and the team asked whether neighbourhood disadvantage and insurance type predict such delay.

Using records from several academic health systems for 2012 to 2024, the cohort held 6,639 patients, median age 62. Median time to surgery was eight days, but 25.3 percent waited beyond fourteen days. Living in the more deprived neighbourhood quartiles, Spanish-speaking status, greater illness burden, and Medicare insurance each independently raised the odds of delay. The authors call for targeted steps to improve access.
pmc-13272885:
Parvaneh Sadeghimoghaddam leads a 2026 study of outcomes after advanced resuscitation for preterm babies in Tehran, Iran. Advanced help at birth included a breathing tube, chest compressions, or epinephrine. The team studied 444 babies born before 33 weeks at one hospital in 2020 and 2021.

Babies who received advanced resuscitation died within 28 days more often, at 26.8 percent against 7.7 percent. They also had more breathing distress, air leaks in the chest, a persistent heart vessel, and bleeding in the brain. The authors urge caution in reading this, since sicker babies are the ones who need such help, and advise careful follow-up of survivors.
pmc-13273385:
Meizhu Gao leads a 2026 review of gut microbe products and their roles in cardiovascular disease, disease of the heart and vessels. The review focuses on three groups: trimethylamine N-oxide, short-chain fatty acids, and bile acids. These chemicals act as signals between the gut and the heart, shaped by diet and by which microbes are present.

Higher levels of the first product link consistently to artery clogging and clot risk, while short-chain fatty acids generally protect vessels and calm inflammation. Bile acids play a dual role, guiding fat handling and inflammatory signaling through dedicated receptors. The authors synthesize evidence on high blood pressure, atherosclerosis, and heart failure to guide new diagnosis and treatment ideas.
pmc-13273985:
Enatfenta Sewmehone Endalew and co-authors report a 2026 qualitative journal article on exercise during pregnancy in Ethiopian cities. Health guidance urges at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week in pregnancy, yet few Ethiopian women reach that level. The team asked what women knew, and what helped or blocked them.

Seven focus group talks were held with forty-five pregnant women at health centers in four cities. Most women knew activity was healthy, but some wrongly feared it could cause abortion early in pregnancy. Walking was the favored activity. Barriers included poor health, busy jobs, fear of judgment, and missing sidewalks. Partner support and access to green space helped women stay active.
pmc-13274585:
Zhaoyuan Yao and a large team report a 2026 journal article presenting BERTH, an artificial intelligence system for watching the global water cycle. Satellites see Earth's surface well, but turning those images into rainfall, soil moisture, and runoff figures usually needs chained models with local tuning. Climate change is making water swings faster and harsher.

BERTH is a transformer model, the architecture behind modern language AI, trained on global data sets. It converts satellite radiance directly into four outputs: evaporation from land, precipitation, soil moisture, and runoff. It maps the whole planet at thirty-meter detail, updated daily. The authors report it beat existing physics-based models on accuracy across varied conditions.
pmc-13274885:
Yang Guo and co-authors present a 2026 journal article mapping the psychology of work alienation among nursing interns in China. Alienation means feeling estranged and powerless at work, a risk during demanding clinical internships. Instead of simple cause-and-effect models, the team built a network of linked factors from 934 valid surveys at four large hospitals in Shaanxi.

Three factors sat at the network's center: personal responsibility, burnout, and feeling unable to protect a patient's best interest. The strongest bridge between clusters was secondary traumatic stress, the strain of absorbing patients' trauma, followed by perceived workload and self-evaluation. Networks did not differ by gender, age, or education. The authors propose these hubs as candidate targets for support programs.
pmc-13276185:
Mostafa Nagy and co-authors present a 2026 case study on hunting gold in Egypt's Central Eastern Desert. Rich gold deposits sit in ancient ophiolitic rocks there, but the cracks and faults that control the ore are poorly mapped. The study focused on the small Um Salim prospect.

The team combined satellite images, airborne magnetic surveys, and structural mapping. Machine learning sorted rock types from detailed light data with high accuracy, one method reaching about ninety-six percent. Magnetic data showed a strong anomaly right over the Um Salim mine, rooted deep below. Line patterns pointed to zones where faults cross and shear, matching known mineralized zones. Depth estimates placed most magnetic bodies within a kilometer of the surface. The authors flag the eastern and southeastern area as top targets for further exploration.
pmc-13276285:
Fitsum Dejene and co-authors report a 2026 laboratory study on two familiar plants as germ fighters. Rue and garlic have long histories in Ethiopian traditional medicine. The team tested alcohol extracts of rue leaves and garlic bulbs against bacteria, including the slimy biofilms bacteria build for protection.

Chemical screening found plant compounds such as phenols, tannins, and alkaloids in the extracts. Both extracts killed all the reference bacteria tested. In dish tests, both also suppressed biofilm growth compared with untreated controls. Light-based analysis picked out the chemical groups present, and elemental tests found minerals like potassium and zinc. The authors say the results back traditional uses. They propose the plants as cheap, natural options for biofilm infections, especially in oral health.
pmc-13276385:
Yueqin Wang and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on why some lung cancers resist targeted drugs by hiding from the immune system. EGFR-blocking drugs help many patients with non-small cell lung cancer, but resistance almost always develops. The team focused on NSUN2, an enzyme that edits RNA, the cell's working copies of genes.

In drug-resistant cancer cells, silencing NSUN2 did nothing when no immune system was present. In animals with working immunity, though, silencing it slowed tumors and restored drug sensitivity. Cold, immune-empty tumors turned hot and immune-rich. The silencing drew in macrophages, immune cells that engulf threats, and pushed them toward their tumor-fighting state. A gene called TRIM29 proved to be the key middleman. The authors identify NSUN2 as a driver of immune evasion and drug resistance.
pmc-13276785:
Chia-Ming Lee and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a microscope for imaging whole cleared organs in three dimensions. Tissue clearing turns organs transparent, but the harsh solvents attack microscope lenses, and standard setups struggle with large samples. Their light-sheet system uses a Bessel beam, a long thin light blade.

The system works with both immersion lenses and capped air lenses. Imaging natural glow in cleared mouse embryos revealed fine anatomy, including kidney tubules at developmental stages. For solvent clearing, the team designed a protective cap that shields the lens and converts a standard air lens into an immersion performer. With it they imaged whole cleared mouse brains at cellular resolution. The design is simplified and open source. The authors aim to widen access to whole-organ developmental imaging.
pmc-13277285:
Mahmoud Azhary leads a 2026 case series on giant tumors behind the abdominal organs, an area called the retroperitoneum. Such tumors grow large before they are found and sit close to vital structures, which makes surgery hard. The team reviewed five patients whose tumors, ten to forty centimeters wide, shared a spindle cell pattern under the microscope.

Diagnoses included a stromal tumor, a desmoid-type growth, and fat tissue cancers. All five had open surgery, sometimes removing parts of nearby organs to clear the tumor fully. No major complications followed, symptoms eased, and no return was seen over about six months. The series shows surgery can be done safely with careful planning, not that cancer control lasts.
pmc-13279485:
Jenny Guo and colleagues report a 2026 study of phone and wearable tracking in teens with depression. Phones and wrist devices can track mood and acts with low burden. Yet long term use past one week in teens with depression was little known. The team ran a one month plan with mood surveys, a wrist act tracker and passive phone sensors.

Sixty nine teens aged twelve to eighteen took part, with mean age near fifteen and a half. Most, at ninety one percent, finished all parts of the plan. The same share would join again, and ninety three percent would tell peers to join. Daily survey response rose from about fifty seven to sixty six percent across the month. Exit talks rated the plan as welcome. Month long tracking looks workable for teen mood research.
pmc-13279585:
Yu Jiang and colleagues give a 2026 narrative review of tetramethylpyrazine in spinal cord injury. Spinal cord injury causes lasting loss of move and feel, a heavy load for patients and families. The compound, called TMP, comes from a plant used in Chinese medicine. It shows wide drug acts in lab work. The review pulls cell, animal and clinical studies on TMP for cord repair.

Eighty six works were summed in all. Listed paths hold nerve regrowth, better vessel flow, less swelling and less nerve cell death. TMP also cut rust like stress, steadied iron and ion balance, and curbed two cell death types. In animal models, cord shape, limb moves and nerve signals improved. Human reports on TMP shots add early clinical hints. The breadth makes TMP a rich test case for multi path repair.
pmc-13279985:
Andrea Du Preez and colleagues present a 2026 randomised feasibility trial of a remote employee health programme in the United Kingdom. Workplaces reach many adults and can support lasting habit change. Diet and activity are usual targets, yet sleep is a strong and neglected health factor. Staff at a higher education site with short sleep, under seven hours, and raised heart risk joined. Twenty eight staff took part in all.

One group got a sleep enhanced plan that joined sleep hygiene, diet and activity advice for fourteen weeks. The other got a standard plan with diet and activity only. Feasibility checks held sign up, stay rates and task follow through. Acceptability came from interviews built on a behaviour theory frame. Self report and device measures tracked sleep, diet, activity and body size. The trial tests if a sleep first design can run well at work before a full trial.
pmc-13280585:
Haryo Kunto Wibisono and team write a 2026 letter on elevating the relevance of autoethnography in end of life care research. They reply to a 2026 article by Neto, which uses the method in end of life care inquiry. That work examines three recurrent interaction patterns in such care, nicknamed The Palliative Honeymoon, The Cousin of France, and Do Everything. Past the clinical insights, the method merits a place in the conversation, the letter argues.

The method stresses personal experience in cultural beliefs, practices, identities and context, with roots in anthropology. It has long held an ambiguous scope in health research, praised for depth and questioned for rigor. Neto showed that analytic use of the method, with systematic reflexivity and scholarly care, can yield knowledge that surveys can not reach. The letter backs wider, careful use in this inquiry, where lived experience is core data.
pmc-13280985:
Alyaa I Eliwa and colleagues tested a soap-like chemical against drug-proof germs in a 2026 lab study. The germ was E coli, a common gut germ that can cause infection. Many strains now shrug off several drugs at once. Much of that strength sits on plasmids, small rings of gene code that germs pass around. The team took samples from hospital patients and grew one hundred ninety strains. Fifty of the toughest strains went into the main test.

The chemical drove the rings out of more than four in five strains. Stripped strains lost much of their drug strength, above all against two key drug families. They also made less of a poison that bursts red blood cells and swam less well. The authors call the method a lab tool for studying how germs gain and lose their power.
pmc-13281885:
Hani M Almoallim and colleagues compared advanced arthritis drugs in Saudi clinics in a 2026 study. Rheumatoid arthritis care aims low: calm the disease fast and hold it there. When plain drugs fall short, doctors step up to biologic or targeted pills. The team drew on a national Saudi database across many centers. They tracked six hundred forty-seven treatment courses over nine advanced drugs. Checks ran at the start, mid-year, and one year, with drug survival tracked to three years.

Disease activity fell clearly over time on the whole. Yet no drug beat the pack in adjusted checks. One-year scores for activity, function, fatigue, and remission clustered tightly across all nine. Stay-on rates were part of the long view as well. The authors say real-world results back a class effect more than a champion drug. Choice, they argue, can rest on safety, cost, and patient fit.
pmc-13282285:
Kodikara Mudiyanselage Chathurika Padmakumari and co-authors present a 2026 case report on combined care for a child with weak tooth enamel on her molars and front teeth. The condition, shortened to MIH, leaves yellow or white patches and raises decay risk. Their patient was an eleven-year-old girl with severe pain in a lower right first molar. Several teeth showed extensive enamel defects and decay.

A team plan mixed prevention, repair, and emotional support. Dentists taught cleaning and diet habits, removed teeth that could not be saved, and filled affected molars. Fluoride varnish and a mineral cream were applied to rebuild enamel. Because past anaesthesia had left her anxious, behaviour strategies were used to calm her. Her pain eased, root canal and filling work finished, and braces treatment began. The authors stress early diagnosis and team care to protect both teeth and quality of life.
pmc-13282385:
Marwa Abou-Taleb and co-authors present a 2026 textile study dyeing wool and polyamide fabrics with a pigment from a fungus. Synthetic dyes are often petroleum based, so natural colourants are sought. The team was first to test pigment production by the fungus Aspergillus turcosus. They extracted its pigment, characterised it with infrared and magnetic resonance methods, and dyed both fabrics under varied conditions.

The pigment bound well to both fabrics, with good resistance to fading. Dyed fabrics gained strong antibacterial action, with clear zones growing from zero to over thirty millimetres. Their antioxidant activity also jumped several-fold against undyed cloth. Sun protection rose sharply for both fabrics. The authors present the pigment as a route to healthier, high-performance textiles that add function while cutting synthetic dye use. Wool suits skin contact, while the synthetic fabric adds strength, so the pairing covers wide garment uses.
pmc-13282485:
Mats Volmer and co-authors present a 2026 quantum computing study on what limits moving electron spins along a silicon chip. Electron spins in silicon are promising building blocks, called qubits, for large quantum computers. A conveyor-belt method shuttles spins between quantum dots, but a property called valley splitting varies unpredictably across the chip and can spoil coherence, the fragile quantum state. The team mapped that property across a small device region.

Valley splitting spanned a huge range, driven by disorder in the silicon-germanium alloy. Where it was low, and at certain resonances, transported spins lost coherence as theory predicts. Rapid, repeated passes through bad spots paradoxically protected coherence, an effect called motional narrowing. By choosing shuttle paths that avoided problem areas, the team moved spins tens of microns with coherence limited by another factor.
pmc-13282685:
Majbaul Alam and co-authors present a 2026 study on how digestion in a lab model changes the antioxidant power of five underused Bangladeshi fruits. The fruits were amla, olive, hog plum, elephant apple, and bilimbi. Antioxidants are compounds that neutralise damaging free radicals linked to chronic disease. Fresh and lab-digested extracts were compared for vitamin C, plant phenols, and several antioxidant tests.

Amla held the most vitamin C and the most flavonoids, a plant compound class, before and after digestion. Elephant apple led on total phenols and on one radical test before digestion, and stayed strong after. Digestion raised flavonoid measures but lowered flavanols and weakened most radical-scavenging scores. One antioxidant test, though, improved after digestion, with amla on top. The authors single out amla and elephant apple for health product development. Their results show digestion can cut or boost measured benefits depending on the compound class.
pmc-13282985:
How deep should a back nerve block go before spine cement surgery? Yujia Liu's 2026 randomized trial compares three depths. The procedure fixes crushed vertebrae with cement and can be painful. A back nerve block plus a low dose of esketamine was used for pain control.

A total of 120 patients were split at random into three groups of 40 each. Groups got a deep block, a shallow block, or both depths combined. The combined group had less pain during surgery and needed less rescue pain relief. Blood pressure and heart signs stayed steadier in that group. Side effects did not differ clearly, and late pain gaps faded by 12 hours.
pmc-13283385:
Research linking gut inflammation to brain disorders has exploded since 2021, Jingwen Li's bibliometric team charts in 2026. Interest in gut-brain links in inflammatory bowel disease has grown fast. The study charts who publishes, where, and on what hot topics.

Records from 2005 to 2024 in a major database gave 2,429 papers for analysis. Output rose steadily and sped up after 2021 in the field. Work came from 62 countries, 2,774 centers, and 12,399 researchers in total. The United States and China led output, with Mayo Clinic and Harvard as hubs. Hot topics center on the gut-brain axis and related mechanisms. Trends point to deeper cross-field work ahead.
pmc-13284485:
Ashok Basnet and co-authors present a 2026 case report of lung paragonimiasis, a foodborne fluke infection, in a 38-year-old man. The illness followed eating crab, a known source when crabs or crayfish are raw or undercooked. Early signs included fever, belly pain, weight loss, fluid near the lung, and very high eosinophil counts.

Two months later the man returned coughing blood with low oxygen. Scans showed cavity-like lung lesions, pleural nodules, and a collapsed lung from trapped air. Parasite eggs in sputum confirmed the diagnosis. Drainage, nebulized treatment, and praziquantel led to improvement. The authors warn that this infection can mimic tuberculosis and urge early testing in endemic areas.
pmc-13284885:
Liepollo Ntlhakana and Mpho Matlakale Molete give a 2026 scoping review on noise-induced hearing loss risk among dental students worldwide. Dental noise is lower than in many jobs, yet training exposes students for years and hearing protection is often weak. The review searched six databases for studies from 2014 to 2025, plus grey sources.

Ten studies met the criteria from sixty-nine first found. Eight reported risk for students, tied in part to high-speed handpieces, with some students noting ringing after use. Only four studies checked what students knew about noise risk, and awareness was poor. The authors urge early checks, risk review, and training on hearing safety at undergraduate level.
pmc-13285585:
Bending stiffness in cochlear implant wires can be dialed by three size choices, Abdulaziz S. Alaboodi and co-authors model in a 2026 computer study. The thin arrays must thread a spiral ear canal without buckling or harm. The team built a virtual beam of metal wires in silicone and bent it in free space, as in surgery, while a planned test grid varied tip radius, base radius, and length.

Across fifteen runs, tip bend and push-back force spanned wide ranges, and peak stress sat at the fixed base, safely below the alloy yield point. Length ruled tip bend, while base radius ruled force. Fit formulas predicted results almost exactly in these clean simulations. The authors offer the map for safer array design.
pmc-13286185:
Jhonatan Silva, Johanne Cohen, and Daniel Cordeiro present GARN3, a refined tool for guessing RNA shapes, in a 2026 methods article. RNA strands fold into three-dimensional forms that decide what they can do in the cell, and lab methods to read those forms cost dearly. Their program treats shape building as a game among strand parts, now with extra anchor points laid along the molecule's spiral sections.

A learning step inside the scoring now estimates gaps between parts, which sharpens each trial shape. On standard test sets the tool matched or beat rival methods for closeness to the true form. Gains showed most clearly on large molecules, where the finer anchors pay off most. Small molecules improved on most of one test set while staying competitive on the harder set, and the code is freely posted for other labs.
pmc-13287285:
Gabriella Bottari reviewed records in 2026 for 25 children with septic shock who received a blood-cleaning cartridge alongside kidney support therapy. The question was how treatment dose should be measured. Dose was expressed as litres of blood cleaned per kilogram of body weight, and cartridge filling over time was modelled.

Median exposure reached 14.4 litres per kilogram, well above adult values reported earlier. Reductions in a key inflammatory signal tracked starting level strongly, not the dose figure. Blood pressure drug needs showed no straight link to dose either. Bottari suggests that past a certain exposure, removal depends mainly on how much inflammatory material is present.
pmc-13288585:
Patrick Weiand and co-authors probe a sugar weakness in blood cancers driven by the JAK2V617F mutation in a 2026 laboratory study. These myeloproliferative neoplasms include polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis, and current drugs control them without curing, so the team searched for metabolic pressure points in cell and mouse models.

Mutant cells burned more glucose under control of the HIF-1 signal, and only removing both GLUT1 and GLUT3 transporters together cut off uptake fully. Blocking glucose entry stalled mutant cells in S phase and killed them, and drug blockade shrank human mutant cell lines in dishes, especially alongside ruxolitinib. In mice, though, transporter blockade shifted blood formation to the spleen without easing core disease features.
pmc-13288685:
Shiwei Song and colleagues rank exercise types for women with extra weight in 2026. Their review searched seven databases. The cut date was September 2025. Only randomized trials were kept. Programs ran from aerobic work to vibration training.

Forty-three trials with 2,315 women were kept. Mixed aerobic and strength work cut body fat. Interval training also cut body fat. Aerobic work at many paces helped too. Hard aerobic work looked best for fat share. It also looked best for body mass index. Intervals led for fat mass alone. No program clearly raised lean mass. Strength work ranked best on that measure, though.
pmc-13288885:
Rashid M Rashid, Dedius E Peter, and Walter C Millanzi survey Tanzanian health students on feeding assessment for older patients in a 2026 cross-sectional study. As the country's population ages fast, they randomly sampled 384 undergraduates in Dodoma and tested knowledge, attitudes, and practical barriers with a structured questionnaire.

Nearly half the students, 47.7 percent of the sample, showed inadequate knowledge, while just over half held positive attitudes and well over half reported serious practical challenges. Prior geriatric training and living with older adults went with better knowledge, and having actually assessed an older patient went with warmer attitudes. More hands-on teaching is the clear implication the authors draw for curricula.
pmc-13289185:
Joshua Xu and colleagues report a 2026 pharmacist-led cholesterol project in West London. The project dealt with patients after heart events. Software flagged those with high cholesterol left. Pharmacists then reviewed each flagged case. Drug doses were raised where needed.

The set held 204 patients in all. Most were men, at 71 percent. Two-thirds came from diverse ethnic groups. Mean cholesterol started at a high level. One in eight took no lowering drug at all. After review, mean levels fell a lot. Seven in ten hit the target level. Gains were even across sex and ethnic groups. The poorest group engaged least, though.
pmc-13289785:
Chunchun Mi and coauthors introduce a 2026 family of metal-free light-driven catalysts built around rubicene, a carbon-rich ring system. Light-driven redox catalysts that avoid metals are cheap and tunable, but many fail in strong acid or base or fade too fast when excited. The new series absorbs visible light and drives substitution and addition reactions in tests.

Trapping tests and fluorescence quenching checks point to single-electron transfer as the working path. The catalysts stayed stable in use and beat commercial metal-free options on reactivity in the comparisons. Broad tolerance across reaction types was also reported for the series. Longer-lived, tougher organic catalysts could widen green synthesis options.
pmc-13290085:
Blocking the protein CD69 slowed leukemia development in mice in a 2026 study led by Yuchen Li and co-authors. The work concerns chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) carrying an Nras G12D mutation, a form tied to shorter survival and a higher risk of turning into acute myeloid leukemia.

Using a mouse model built around that single mutation, the team mapped changes in the bone marrow environment and gave some animals an antibody against CD69. Treated mice showed fewer granulocyte-macrophage progenitor cells, longer survival, and less buildup of regulatory T cells in the marrow. The findings point to CD69 as a marker of immune dysfunction in the marrow niche and a possible treatment target.
pmc-13290185:
A new hydrogel wound template reached skin grafting unusually fast in a 2026 pilot study by Eric Clayman and colleagues. The product, DermiSphere, mixes a collagen hydrogel scaffold with collagen microspheres and is meant to prepare facial defects for a second-stage graft after cancer removal.

Four patients with facial defects (two nasal, one forehead, one cheek) received the template in one or two layers once margins were clear. Every wound built a vascularized bed quickly, and grafting followed 7 to 18 days later, averaging 11.5 days before the second stage. Wounds contracted somewhat without distorting nearby tissue, and results kept improving over time. Clayman and colleagues say the early series supports the template's use, while noting the group was very small.
pmc-13290385:
Feedback during residency can build confidence or quietly crush it, and a 2026 qualitative study by Abrar Alabdulghafour and colleagues looks at how pediatric trainees in Kuwait live that experience. Earlier work leaned on questionnaires; this study asked people directly.

The researchers interviewed eleven pediatric residents who trained between 2015 and 2020, plus three supervisors, and analyzed the transcripts for themes. Five emerged, covering what shapes feedback, its effects, how trainees learn to give it, what received feedback looks like, and where the process breaks down. Supportive feedback lifted confidence and learning, while harsh or vague feedback bred demotivation. Hierarchy, ward culture, and workload pressures colored nearly every account, giving program leaders concrete places to intervene.
pmc-13290585:
Better teaching at discharge leaves eye surgery patients readier to go home, and Yuanyuan Wang and colleagues trace the route in a 2026 study. Their patients had surgery for diabetic retinopathy in Weifang, Shandong, where shorter stays push more recovery into the home.

Surveying 489 patients, the team scored teaching quality, discharge readiness, social support, and psychological resilience, then modeled the pathways between them. Teaching quality correlated with all three other measures. Mediation analysis showed support and resilience passing the effect along in a chain: well-taught patients drew more support, felt hardier, and so felt readier, with the chain carrying 36.38% of the total association across the group. The authors advise nurses to build support systems and resilience, not just hand over instructions.
pmc-13290685:
International medical students in Britain see injustice clearly but feel powerless to fight it, Shafeena Anas and colleagues report in a qualitative study from 2026 framed by Paulo Freire's critical pedagogy. The team explored how these students grasp social justice and their own room to act.

Three online focus groups with 11 second-year international students produced four themes. Students showed early critical consciousness, naming how poverty, racism, disability, and immigration status shape health. General practice placements exposed them to language barriers and strained services, confirming inequity as systemic. Inside their school they felt financial and representational unfairness, yet stable team-based groups and supportive staff gave them belonging. Still, hierarchy and scarce resources left awareness without agency. The authors argue medical schools must turn reflection into real routes for action.
pmc-13290985:
Nursing care built around clear sedation goals is tested in a 2026 randomized trial by Xi Luo and Huafu Zhang. The children were having a bronchoalveolar lavage done with topical anesthesia plus procedural sedation. Comfort during the wash procedure was the main outcome, with cooperation and several safety measures also tracked.

A total of 168 children entered the trial, and 163 remained in the final analysis after exclusions. Children in the bundle group had lower discomfort scores and better cooperation rates than controls, and more of them reached an ideal sedation level during the work. Procedure time also ran shorter in the bundle group. The findings support structured, goal-led nursing as a practical way to make a stressful airway procedure easier for children.
pmc-13291085:
Eight years of growing tomatoes on a Barcelona rooftop greenhouse are summed up in a 2026 case study led by Guido Evangelista. Management changed step by step over that span, as the team chased higher yields with less water, fewer mined fertilizers, and lower overall environmental cost in an integrated city building.

Yield, sunlight, water and nutrient use, and life cycle impacts were tracked across cycles with different feeding and lighting choices. Best output came in 2023 after worn roof panels were replaced and more sunlight entered, in cycles fed with recovered struvite or standard mineral fertilizer alike. Impact per tomato fell most where yields ran high, showing that good light and careful feeding can cut footprint without cutting the harvest.
pmc-13291185:
Students watching doctors at work need better ground rules. Molly Estes leads a 2026 study to set best practice for shadowing in emergency care. Watching care is often a student’s first taste of real medicine. Most past guidance spoke to students, not to the doctors hosting them.

Ten emergency teachers with advising roles formed the panel. They first drafted a long list of ideas. Four rounds of private voting cut the list down. Ten shared recommendations won full backing in the end. Themes stressed clear structure and safe roles for guests. Busy, high-risk wards need such rules most. The list gives hosts a shared starting point.
pmc-13291785: Ping Huang and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their study on predicting outcomes in multiple myeloma using bone marrow cell shape, vitamin D, and interleukin-6. The notice fixes the ethics approval number for the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University, which should read CY2025-344-01 rather than the printed number. The corrected passage also restates the second hospital's approval and notes that written consent came from all participants. The original article has been updated. Only the correction is available here, so the study cannot be summarized from it.
pmc-13292385:
Waqas Haider and a large team set out a 2026 green extraction study on polysaccharides from Melastoma dodecandrum, a plant eaten and used in traditional remedies across South China. Its extracts are reported to calm inflammation and influence blood sugar and lipids, but its polysaccharides remain little studied. The team applies ultrasound-assisted extraction with a deep eutectic solvent instead of plain hot water.

The work optimizes the process with response surface methodology and an artificial neural network, then examines extraction kinetics and the product's structure. Cellular antioxidant activity testing rounds out the plan described. The study aims to show that a solvent kinder to the environment can pull these large sugar chains efficiently while keeping their useful properties. That would strengthen the case for developing the plant's polysaccharides for food and health uses.
pmc-13292585:
Licheng Li and a large team expose a 2026 survival trick in multiple myeloma: the transcription factor E4BP4 gags the cell's self-cleaning and self-killing programs. Database checks showed E4BP4 overexpressed in myeloma tissue and in the U266 cell line versus normal blood cells. Lab manipulations then traced how it rewires two death pathways at once.

Extra E4BP4 switched on the deacetylase HDAC3, which stripped acetyl marks from the Beclin1 promoter and silenced that autophagy gene, while mTOR signaling rose. The net effect: less autophagy, less apoptosis, and blunted sensitivity to dexamethasone, a backbone myeloma drug. Knocking E4BP4 down restored drug response and shrank mouse xenograft tumors, with the drug combination adding further benefit. The authors nominate E4BP4 as a target for breaking steroid resistance.
pmc-13293385:
Beatriz Cristina Dias de Oliveira and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, new ways to study how Leishmania parasites respond to drugs beyond simple resistance. Treatment failure and relapse stay common in leishmaniasis, yet germ changes alone do not explain them.

Responses also include extra sensitivity, tolerance, and persister cells that survive without gene changes. New genome tools and cell-perturbation methods can split these states apart if trials are designed with them in mind. Careful drug dosing, varied exposure plans, and hunting rare persisters are stressed. The authors frame a fuller view of drug response to guide better therapy research.
pmc-13293785:
Kaja Teraž and colleagues study, in a 2026 mixed-methods paper, whether Mediterranean diet habits link to body makeup and recovery after severe COVID-19 hospitalization. Food and lifestyle may shape rehab, yet their role after discharge is little studied.

Thirty-nine patients in Slovenia were checked at discharge and after eight weeks of self-guided recovery. Fat-free mass rose over time, and higher diet adherence went with more fat-free mass in the authors' analysis. Interviews showed that strong adherers kept steady routines, coped adaptively, and felt more resilient. Diet-based support may aid post-illness recovery programs.
pmc-13293985:
Infanta Saleth Teresa Eden M. and Umashankar Vetrivel present a 2026 method for gene enrichment analysis in organisms that lack good annotations. Popular tools work well for model species but falter for many microbes, and borrowing labels by similarity can add errors and miss unique functions. Their fix builds custom annotation packages in R from NCBI genome data.

As a demonstration, a package for Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv was used with clusterProfiler on RNA data covering six samples, three untreated and three exposed to rifampicin for 1 h. The workflow scales to other poorly annotated species and keeps enrichment tied to each organism's own genes.
pmc-13294185:
Xin Yao and coauthors rank groin hernia operations for older adults in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Best technique for patients aged 60 and older was unsettled, so randomized trials through February 2025 were pooled across four databases. Altogether 28 trials covered 3,184 patients, mostly men with ages spanning 62 to 76 years, and bias varied widely.

Keyhole methods led on recovery measures. One laparoscopic route gave least bleeding and shortest stay, and the earliest walking, while another keyhole route also cut bleeding, stay, and complications. Recurrence matched across methods except one lightweight open repair with higher risk. Best pain relief came from a different approach, so trade-offs remain.
pmc-13294685:
Li-Juan Zhang and co-authors describe freshwater fungi in the genus Neohelicomyces in a 2026 study from Guizhou Province, China. Such fungi live on submerged rotting wood and help break down material in streams and other fresh waters. Six specimens were gathered during field surveys of local habitats.

Microscope examination plus family trees built from several gene regions sorted the collections into three species. Two proved new to science, named N. brevis and N. wujiangensis, while N. astrictus was found in fresh water for the first time. Differences in spore-bearing structures, spore size, and colonies separate the new species from close relatives.
pmc-13295485:
Hamit Çağlayan Kahraman and colleagues test a strengthened tendon stitch in a 2026 lab study. Ligament grafts with free tendon ends must be sewn to holding devices before knee surgery. Adding a periosteum layer to a triple-pass Krackow stitch was compared with two standard sewing patterns.

Cow knee tendons, ten per group, were cycled hundreds of times and then pulled until they failed. The periosteum version withstood clearly higher final loads than both the plain triple-pass and the five-pass versions. Stretch during cycling and stiffness matched across groups, so the gain came without obvious downsides. Surgeons gain a stronger graft preparation option from the result.
pmc-13295785:
Chen Wang and colleagues uncover how a steroid drug wakes anti-tumour immunity in myeloma in a 2026 study. Dexamethasone is a backbone myeloma drug, yet steroids usually damp immunity, making its pairing with immune therapy puzzling. The DNA-sensing STING pathway, often silenced in myeloma, sits at the centre of the answer.

In resting cancer cells, the steroid receptor holds a phosphatase against a signalling pair, keeping STING switched off. Dexamethasone binding breaks that grip within moments, restarting interferon signals. Immune profiling showed fiercer natural killer cells and friendlier macrophage types, all lost when STING was removed, and a phosphatase blocker copied the benefit.
pmc-13295985:
Maria Tibbs and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for reviewing school lessons that teach teenagers to handle media with wellbeing in mind. Phones and social platforms bring connection but also risks, and schools could deliver such lessons widely, though designs vary a lot.

The review will gather studies of pupils aged eleven to eighteen from many databases plus grey sources. Effects on mental, social, physical and digital wellbeing will be pooled with a multilevel method, while lesson content and delivery get a narrative summary. Findings will be shared in a journal paper and at conferences.
pmc-13296585:
Lithium disilicate veneers get a 2026 review from Silvia Rojas-Ruedas and co-authors, thin ceramic shells bonded to the front of teeth for smile repair. They summarise strength, looks and gluing methods from the literature and add two treated cases showing the workflow.

The ceramic bends without breaking at high loads, looks natural and bonds reliably when enamel is kept and bonding steps are followed carefully. Reported survival passes ninety-five percent at ten years in selected patients. Failures such as loosening and chipping cluster where enamel is scarce or bite risks are unmanaged. Careful case choice drives success, the authors stress.
pmc-13296885:
Kangrong Liu and co-authors build, in 2026, a brain-inspired neural network for fire detection from fused sensor readings. False alarms and missed fires plague multi-sensor systems thanks to noise and mixed sensor types, so the team adapt a coupled network with a global threshold tuning its activity.

Training used rebalanced data reshaped into matrices, and the model scored near-perfect accuracy on both the team's own dataset and a public smoke detection set. The authors present the design as a step toward smarter building safety systems that can tell real fires from cooking steam and dust.
pmc-13297185:
Zhi-Wei Ye and co-authors test, in 2026, a small molecule, SC18, that jams a channel in melanoma cell powerhouses. The channel is plentiful in melanoma and marks worse outlook, so pigmented and pale cell lines from humans and mice were dosed and watched.

The drug dropped membrane voltage and oxygen use, drained energy stores and piled up damaging oxygen chemistry and fat oxidation. Cells survived and migrated less, with pale cells hit hardest, and standard chemotherapy paired well with it. The authors propose the channel as a metabolic weak point worth exploiting.
pmc-13297785:
A cartridge-based test panel identified dengue accurately and typed its serotypes in a two-phase evaluation led by Stephany Young Yusty in 2026. The STANDARD M10 panel also screens for Zika, chikungunya, yellow fever, and West Nile viruses, which circulate together across the Americas and cause look-alike fevers.

Against a composite reference standard, the panel scored 96.0% sensitivity and 100% specificity on 163 stored serum samples, with agreement of κ = 0.95. Serotype 3 dominated the positives at 77.1%. Dilution tests showed detection limits matching or beating reference PCR for six of eight targets, though DENV-2 and chikungunya needed higher concentrations. The authors back the panel as a decentralized aid, noting formal detection-limit studies are still missing.
pmc-13298685:
COVID-19 in Brazil's Ceará state kept spreading even as it grew far less deadly, quantify Matheus Paiva Emidio Cavalcanti and co-authors in a 2026 modeling study. Using official surveillance data from 2020 to 2023, they fitted generalized linear models with the pandemic's first year as the baseline.

Infection risk stayed elevated through 2022, with a rate ratio of 1.42, while mortality risk fell 68% by 2022 and 99% by 2023. Fatality risk among cases dropped steadily, reaching a 91% reduction in 2023. The authors read the split as a transition toward lower severity and stress resilient health systems and fair vaccine access.
pmc-13299385:
Immunotherapy given around bladder surgery is redrawing treatment for muscle-invasive disease, review Albert Jang and colleagues in a 2026 article. Tumors that have reached the bladder muscle still recur often after removal, and chemotherapy before surgery leaves many patients relapsing.

Checkpoint inhibitors have now won approvals in three slots: nivolumab after surgery, and durvalumab or pembrolizumab paired with a targeted drug in sandwich regimens spanning before and after the operation. The review walks through the trials behind each approval and the ones still running. It closes on the field's open argument, how to avoid overtreating patients already cured by surgery while not undertreating the rest, and the need for predictive biomarkers.
pmc-13299585:
Road asphalt fortified with a rubbery polymer tires in a pattern that engineers can now model precisely, report Chenze Fang and co-authors in a 2026 study. SBS modifier forms a three-dimensional gel network inside asphalt, and the team ran repeated indirect tensile tests to watch damage accumulate.

Residual strain after each load cycle tracked fatigue cracking closely, tying damage to the material's permanent, viscoplastic deformation. Their damage-informed model reproduced the nonlinear strain response, and a new indicator, the relative residual strain change rate, gauged resistance to cracking. The authors explain the polymer network's protection and offer the model for pavement design.
pmc-13301085:
Electron microscope images of nerves refuse to match across laboratories, and Vitalijs Borisovs with Guido Cavaletti built a deep-learning pipeline to tame them in a 2026 methods study. Their preprocessing, blending contrast equalization with noise suppression inside commercial software, harmonized three very different staining traditions, from osmium Palade to uranium-free lanthanide methods.

A U-Net trained on just fifteen composite images scored above 0.95 overlap for myelin and Schwann cells at home. Sent zero-shot into forty unseen images, it still held a Dice score of 0.854 for myelin, though mitochondria proved harder at 0.597 overall. The open tools support greener staining and unlock dusty clinical archives.
pmc-13301185:
A banana plant's own stray DNA can vaccinate or betray it, depending on how sick the donor leaf was. Yuxuan Hu and colleagues test that twist in a 2026 study of extracellular self-DNA against Fusarium wilt, the tropical race 4 scourge of banana farms. Hydroponic plants received DNA from leaves at different disease stages.

DNA from mildly diseased tissue held back fungal colonization, supported growth, and eased oxidative harm. DNA from severely diseased leaves lost that shield and even deepened cell stress. Helpful DNA cut peroxide and damage markers while lifting antioxidant enzymes, and gene profiling showed wide reprogramming toward metabolic balance. Stage-aware DNA signals may seed greener wilt controls.
pmc-13302185:
Where an analyst draws the heart's edge changes what a flow scan reports, Alexander Gall and colleagues quantify in a 2026 methods study of 4D flow cardiac MRI. Five cases were segmented by deep learning, then re-measured with contours pulled inward by one and two voxels. Kinetic energy, vorticity, and viscous energy loss were compared across the three masks.

Shrinking the mask cut every measure. Kinetic energy fell about eighteen and thirty-five percent at the two steps, tracking lost volume. Gradient-based measures swung harder: left ventricular vorticity dropped from 249.6 to 157.0 per second at two voxels, with energy loss falling in step. The authors recommend one standard inward step for all pipelines.
pmc-13303185:
The discarded tops of a prized medicinal orchid outperform its famous tuber in the test tube, Yuru Zhang and colleagues find in a 2026 metabolomics comparison. Six parts of Gastrodia elata, from stem and capsule shell above ground to seed and three tuber zones below, were profiled by mass spectrometry. Extracts were then assayed for antioxidant power and alpha-glucosidase blocking, a diabetes-relevant activity.

Chemical fingerprints split cleanly between above-ground and underground tissues. Stems and capsule shells, normally thrown away, showed the strongest antioxidant and enzyme-blocking activity, beating the conventional tuber. Two amino acids, L-arginine and L-aspartate, tracked the activity differences. The authors urge fuller use of the whole plant.
pmc-13303585:
Huimin Tian and colleagues share a 2026 case report with a literature review on anti-GBM disease, a rare immune disorder that attacks the kidneys and lungs. Standard care pairs plasma exchange with immune-suppressing drugs, but kidneys often fail when disease is already severe.

One very ill patient had no urine output, badly raised creatinine, high antibody levels, and widespread crescent damage on kidney biopsy. Plasma exchange was continued until the harmful antibodies were fully cleared, alongside immune-suppressing treatment. Kidney function recovered and stayed normal through five years of follow-up. The case suggests that early and persistent exchange may rescue even poor-outlook kidneys.
pmc-13304485:
Shusen Wang and co-authors build a layered electrode for supercapacitors, fast-charge storage devices, in a 2026 materials study. The design grows nickel-manganese oxide particles over nickel-cobalt oxide sheets on nickel foam, with no binder needed.

A two-step microwave water-heating method plus baking formed the lacy sheet frame and its particle coat. Holding time in the second step was varied across four values. The middle holding time gave the roomiest surface, the strongest charge storage, and fair endurance across thousands of cycles. Wide open pores and short ion paths explain the winning performance.
pmc-13306585:
Otman Saud loaded a chemotherapy drug into vesicles taken from bowel cancer patients in a 2026 study. Natural cell vesicles may carry drugs with less whole-body harm, yet cancer stage and the protein coat around each vesicle could change performance.

Vesicles came from blood and tissue of patients at differing stages plus healthy controls, each group showing distinct profiles in reported checks. Cancer vesicles loaded more doxorubicin than healthy ones, and tissue vesicles carried the most drug-loaded particles. Uptake into two cancer cell lines also shifted with disease stage and protein coat.
pmc-13307185:
Felix Kwashie Madilo checked hygiene and germ safety of raw beef at Ho Central Market in Ghana in a 2026 study. Sixty-three handlers and facilities across 25 shops answered structured questions, while twelve beef samples were taken twice daily in duplicate.

Standard lab counts covered total bacteria, staphylococci and gut families, plus targeted hunts for E. coli O157 and Salmonella types. Watchers found food safety and hygiene standards compromised at stalls in reported observations, even where personal habits such as protective clothing looked better. The work links daily handling gaps to pathogen risk in market beef.
pmc-13307385:
Hui Liu, Hong Tan, and Li Li study in 2026 why patients on peritoneal dialysis in Xinjiang, China, often miss their medicines, and they build a short risk model. Their survey covered 401 patients on home based dialysis, with scales for self care, confidence, and feelings of helplessness.

Poor adherence was common, at 286 of the 401 patients in the group studied here. A LASSO method kept just three signals: drug side effects, self care level, and helplessness. The short model matched fuller models on accuracy while staying simple to read. Clinics could use it to find high risk patients early and offer focused help.
pmc-13308985:
Sophia Assirlikian and co-authors hunt in 2026 signs that a cervix loop cut will hold no high grade lesion, in women whose biopsy had shown one. Records from nine hospitals held 2037 patients treated from 2015 to 2021, and the cut tissue was checked for what grade, if any, stayed.
