No high grade lesion showed in 191 patients, which is 9.4 percent of the full group in this study. Three signs foresaw that blank: a small odd zone of one quarter or less, a calm scope view, and calm or low grade cell tests. Teams should weigh all three before a cut, since each hints the biopsy may have cleared the spot or overstated it.
pmc-13309985:
Milla Perros and co-authors measure tumor blood flow in lymphoma patients at rest and during exercise in a 2026 study. Exercise is advised for cancer patients, but its instant effect on tumor blood flow in humans had never been measured. Flow matters because it feeds tumors and carries drugs to them.

Eight lymphoma patients, of Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin types, underwent water-based PET scans lying still and again while pedaling gently for ten minutes. Baseline flow in the main tumors ran high. During exercise, flow itself barely changed, while tumor blood volume fell and vessel resistance trended upward in the reported results. Flow change tracked with age and tumor size, not heart rate. The authors offer first human numbers for this question.
pmc-13310385:
Chaowalit Monton and co-authors develop a fingerroot extract mouth spray against tooth decay germs in a 2026 study. Fingerroot, a ginger relative, attacks Streptococcus mutans, the main decay bacterium. Turning its extract into a stable, pleasant spray takes careful tuning of extraction and mixing.

A grid design tuned sound-assisted extraction across time, solvent ratio, and alcohol strength, landing on settings that yielded the most of three active flavonoids. Spray mixes of water, a solvent aid, and alcohol were then tuned, with sweetener and mint added for taste. The finished sprays killed the decay germ in lab tests. Over storage, acidity and flavonoid levels drifted down while germ killing held. The authors report a workable formula path.
pmc-13310785:
Yu Yang and colleagues pool past studies on kidney injury after major aorta surgery in a 2026 review. Surgery for a torn aorta, called type A dissection, often harms the kidneys. The team summed how often harm occurs and which traits raise the risk across the world.

Forty four studies held 11,983 patients in total, and about half showed kidney harm after surgery. The pooled rate reached 50.72 percent of cases when strict rules were used, with higher rates in Chinese studies. Older age, male sex, high weight, high pressure, and longer bypass time raised risk. Early guards for the kidneys may cut harm.
pmc-13310885:
Jiaqi Tian and colleagues link a pale line on X rays to fracture timing in children with bowed shin bones in a 2026 study. Born bowing of the tibia can precede a hard to heal break, and a low density line marks the weak zone. How the size of that line relates to break risk over time was unclear.

Records covered 40 children treated at Hunan Children Hospital from 2015 to 2020. Breaks occurred in 31 children, most within six months of line finding. Larger line share meant far shorter time to break, with median times dropping from over a year to near three months. Line size may guide watch timing.
pmc-13310985:
Burcu Bozkaya Yücel and co-authors track early IL-1 blocking care in childhood Still disease in a 2026 cohort study. The severe swelling disease can trigger a dangerous immune storm, and early targeted care may change its long course. Records from one center for 2018 to 2025 were reviewed.

Eighteen children were followed, with onset at a median age of 6.5 years in the group. Nearly all began with IL-1 blocking drugs, though many switched due to daily shot burden. Quiet disease rose from few at one month to nearly all by six months. The immune storm hit early in many but never returned. Two thirds later stopped all treatment in remission.
pmc-13311185:
Simo Karhi and colleagues test how treatment delay shifts perfusion scan cutoffs in stroke in a 2026 study. Perfusion scans estimate dead brain core at arrival to guide clot removal, yet the best flow cutoff may drift as time to vessel opening grows. Past cases at one center were rechecked against later infarct size.

Among 555 treated patients, 236 with major vessel blocks were included, and 102 gained full flow return. For fast return within about 100 minutes, lower flow cutoffs matched later size best with less overshoot. For return within two hours, a higher cutoff matched best. Cutoff choice should weigh expected delay.
pmc-13311985:
Tingting Lin and co-authors review how the ovary's immune setting governs ovarian aging in a 2026 article. The ovary remodels itself every cycle, and immune cells do much of that work.

The review joins immune and hormone signals across egg growth and follicle ripening, then contrasts healthy aging with early ovarian failure. Shared immune signatures link the two states as points on one path. Treatments under study aim to rebalance defender and regulator cells, redirect macrophage modes, or remodel the niche with stem cells and platelet-rich plasma. The frame could guide therapies that protect fertility and long-term health.
pmc-13312885:
Jheng-Yan Wu and colleagues compare, in a 2026 real-world cohort study, two families of blood pressure drugs in people on maintenance dialysis. Guidelines treat ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers as interchangeable for these patients, but head-to-head cardiovascular evidence in the dialysis population was thin, so the team mined the TriNetX multi-institution network.

Adults with end-stage kidney disease who newly started either drug between 2006 and 2025 were matched one to one, leaving 55,894 patients. Over the first year, those starting a receptor blocker suffered fewer major cardiovascular events than those starting an ACE inhibitor, 30.3 percent against 35.0 percent in the reported figures, with lower stroke and death rates and similar heart attack and potassium outcomes. Checks designed to expose hidden bias came back clean. The authors caution that observation alone cannot prove cause.
pmc-13313085:
Adrielly Cristina de Lima Raimundo and colleagues ask, in a 2026 qualitative study, how neonatal intensive care staff in Brazil see parents taking part in the care of their premature babies. Bringing parents into the unit promises calmer families and stronger bonding, but fear on both sides can keep parents at the glass. The team interviewed the professionals who would have to open the door.

Twenty-six members of the multidisciplinary teams at two intensive care units in Maceió spoke in March 2025. Their accounts sorted into two themes: a passage between fear and discovery, and providing care while promoting bonding. Staff described deliberately folding parents into daily routines to shrink their fear and widen the benefits for the infant, especially through skin-to-skin kangaroo care. The authors argue that warm welcome, clear guidance, and humanization policies turn parental presence into shared responsibility.
pmc-13313185:
Matthew Saunders leads a large team that tackled antibody polyreactivity, the broad weak binding to off-target matter that can make a drug fail fast in the body. Their 2026 paper deals with two linked problems: lab tests for this trait vary a lot, and computer models often fail to spot clean variants near a known drug.

The group refined low- and high-throughput assays so they give steady, shared data sets for training. They then tested how much fine-tuning a protein language model on local data helps it pick non-polyreactive variants inside the narrow sequence space of a real drug program. Summed scores from antibody tests at several strengths gave highly repeatable ground truth. The approach aims to cut failed candidates early, before costly lab work.
pmc-13314885:
Xiaobo Tang and colleagues report a rare tumor behind the chest that masqueraded as lymphoma, in a case study published in 2026. Myeloid sarcoma is a mass of young myeloid cells outside the marrow, often tied to acute myeloid leukemia, and a lone chest mass of this kind is very rare.

Their patient was a 39-year-old man with back pain and chest discomfort. Standard scans showed a smooth mass in the rear chest wrapping the descending aorta, and lymphoma was the first guess. A dual-energy CT scan added clues: low iodine uptake and a flat energy curve that set the mass apart, as the authors report. Surgery and tissue plus stain tests settled the true diagnosis. The case backs dual-energy scanning as a tiebreaker when chest masses mislead.
pmc-13315085:
Mohsen Bagheri and colleagues report a rare spread of lymph vessel tumors across belly organs in a 2026 case study. Lymphangioma of the liver is an extremely rare benign growth, above all in adults, and its cysts can mimic parasite cysts or other cystic diseases on scans.

Their patient was a 40-year-old man with months of belly discomfort and mild swelling, normal lab tests, and no tenderness. Ultrasound showed many cysts through the liver, and CT plus MRI found matching cysts in the spleen and the space behind the belly. The largest sat by the psoas muscle in front of the spine, creeping in the manner typical of this tumor, as the authors describe. Surgery and tissue study proved lymphangioma. The case shows why tissue proof ends most hunts for this diagnosis.
pmc-13316085:
Man Yao and colleagues sorted in 2026 the varied mouth opening problems that follow oral cancer surgery, using latent profile analysis. They recruited 305 operated patients at a Changsha cancer hospital between April and September 2025 and measured maximum opening between the teeth directly.

Questionnaires covered jaw stiffness symptoms and fear of jaw movement. Three groups emerged, with good function and mild symptoms in 86 patients, moderate dysfunction with pain in 153 patients, and severe dysfunction with severe symptoms in 66 patients. Preoperative opening limits raised the odds of landing in worse groups, guiding targeted rehabilitation.
pmc-13316185:
Pranav Padmanabhan and colleagues studied in 2026 what happened when Pueblo, Colorado briefly banned syringe distribution in May 2024. Syringe programs cut HIV and overdose among people who use drugs, and the city ban, driven by litter complaints, lasted three weeks before being overturned in June.

Data from one program and city litter pickups from January to September 2024 were analyzed with interrupted time series methods. During the ban the program logged on average 31 fewer visits, 23 fewer naloxone kits, and 2,406 fewer syringes given out each week, even though other services stayed open. Weekly litter pickup counts were tracked alongside the program data.
pmc-13316285:
Ye Li and co-authors, in a 2026 study, ask how city growth combines with behavior and surroundings to shape lung cancer rates around the world. Their work links personal-level risk factors with broader social and land conditions across many nations.

Records came from GBD 2021 and the World Bank for 187 countries over 1991 to 2021, studied with a spatial learning method paired with explanation tools. Cancer occurrence moved away from older industrial regions toward places urbanizing fast. Pairings of city growth with job exposure led in 103 countries, while pairings with forest cover led in 33 countries. Dirty air raised risk in fast-growing settings, and tree cover often softened it. Prevention, they suggest, must fit each place.
pmc-13316585:
Frederic St-Denis-Bissonnette and a large Ottawa team report 2026 work on tiny packages released by natural killer cells, the immune system's fast killers of cancer cells. Earlier work showed these packages can kill tumors directly; here the question was whether they also retrain other immune cells.

Blood immune cells from healthy donors and cancer patients were exposed to the packages, then read cell by cell and tested against tumors. Gene activity shifted widely in killer T cells and natural killer cells, and tumor killing rose across all donors. Follow-up tests pinned the gain on natural killer cells rather than T cells. The packages look like a cell-free therapy candidate that could be made at scale.
pmc-13316785:
Shuang Qu, Shiping Hu, Jun Zhu, and Huan Ye built a 2026 machine learning model to spot tuberculosis hiding in patients with pneumoconiosis, the lung scarring caused by dust at work. The two diseases overlap in symptoms and scans, so early, accurate sorting guides care.

Records for 325 patients from three Beijing hospitals, admitted between January 2019 and June 2024, split into those with and without tuberculosis. Ten factors stood out, spanning dust history, blood nutrition and sugar markers, and scan features such as cavities and fluid. Eight learning models were trained on those factors and checked with standard accuracy and usefulness curves, with an explanation tool to show each factor's weight. The work supports earlier, data-led diagnosis in chest clinics.
pmc-13317585:
Katherine Cuenca-León and colleagues developed, in a 2026 bench study, a mouth treatment blending three essential oils against Candida albicans, the yeast behind oral thrush, which increasingly resists standard drugs. The oils came from lemongrass, coriander, and oregano plants gathered in southern Ecuador.

Chemical profiling found 40 compounds, led by carvacrol at 30.01 percent of the mix in the measured profile. On agar plates, the blend at ten percent strength in alcohol cleared a zone of 77.89 millimeters, far beyond both chlorhexidine and fluconazole controls in the same test. A water version also worked, though more weakly. The authors call for strength and safety testing before any clinical use.
pmc-13318285:
Luke S. Wimpy leads a 2026 survey experiment on which short messages move public views about the safety of gene editing in farming and medicine. It closes a longer project that began with focus groups and three earlier surveys.

A national sample of 3,200 adults in the United States was randomly shown one of eight videos. Versions differed by speaker, either a researcher or a blogger, by framing around years of safe use or counts of safety studies, and by whether farming or medicine featured. Viewers generally responded well, and what they remembered depended most on the application setting, since recall was stronger when the message matched its field. Speaker and framing choices mattered far less.
pmc-13319085:
Katherine A. Hirchak and colleagues present a 2026 study adapting alcohol-use harm surveys for American Indian and Alaska Native adults. Standard tools miss the history and culture of Indigenous communities. A panel of Indigenous researchers and clinicians reviewed two existing tools. Twenty adults who had drunk heavily or were in recovery were then interviewed.

The panel advised removing 20 items from the longer inventory. It added 12 items to the shorter companion tool and three new subscales. Wording based on strengths replaced stigmatising phrasing throughout. The interviews produced three themes, covering reactions to items, community-specific harms, and recovery supports. Culture, prevention, and wider social factors moved to the centre. The adapted tools will next be tested with 150 adults drawn from across the country.
pmc-13319385:
Yoshiko Toyoda and co-authors present a case report from 2026 about a rare soft tissue tumor in a young woman. The 19 year old had long been told she had a vessel tangle at her right elbow and wrist. She had mild pain, a tingling sign in her forearm, a stiff elbow, and weak turning of the hand.

Fresh scans plus a guided needle sample named the true cause as a calcifying tumor of tendon sheets, found at two sites at once. Cuts to remove both lumps confirmed the call. Nerve squeeze and a worn joint surface came with it, a rare mix. The case warns that this tumor can mimic vessel faults for years.
pmc-13319485:
Katrina Holmes à Court and co-authors explore thinking complaints in body image illness in a 2026 study across clinic and public groups. People with this illness fixate on flaws in how they look that others barely see. What they report about their own thinking speed, focus, and memory had barely been mapped before this work.

One small clinic group of 15 patients was set next to 29 healthy peers, and a far larger public group of 433 people with strong symptoms answered the same new scale. Complaints spanned speed, focus, memory, planning, and reading others, with slow speed standing out most. Clinic patients scored far above peers. Complaints rose most for social thinking when symptoms flared.
pmc-13319885:
Hsiu-Ting Chien and co-authors measure the burden of a rare severe skin illness in Taiwan in a 2026 claims study. The illness brings wide sheets of small pus filled bumps plus body wide swelling, and flares can return again and again. National insurance records were used to count cases, care use, and costs next to a matched group with common plaque skin illness.

A total of 245 people with the rare illness and no prior common plaque illness were found from 2017 onward, with more than a thousand mid to severe flares among them. Their flare rate ran higher than the matched group, and clinic, emergency, and hospital use all ran higher too. Monthly care costs ran about twice as high, which shows the heavy load this rare illness places.
pmc-13320485:
Anna E Sri and co-authors share a 2026 interview study on careful drug use in remote Indigenous communities in Australia. Fourteen nurses, doctors, Aboriginal health workers, vets, and pharmacists spoke about germs that resist antibiotics and how human, animal, and land health link together. Remote clinics face thin staffing and hard choices about when drugs are truly needed.

Staff shortages and heavy workloads made careful prescribing hard, while local health workers helped good practice take hold. Drug use in local animal care was mostly low, though preventive drugs around surgery could improve. Workers showed clear grasp of wider drivers of resistance and a wish to act jointly across health fields.
pmc-13321585:
Gaowa Ailun and co-authors report a rare ovarian cancer in a young woman in a 2026 case report. Ovarian carcinosarcoma mixes two cancer types and is highly aggressive; it mostly strikes women after menopause, so a premenopausal case is uncommon. Clear best treatment is still not settled for this rare tumour.

The patient was a 33-year-old Han Chinese woman treated with full tumour removal surgery followed by platinum based chemotherapy. Gene tests for BRCA faults and repair deficiency came back negative. After a good response, the PARP drug olaparib was started as an individual off-label choice with consent. Disease stayed controlled over 46 months of follow-up without major side effects.
pmc-13321785:
Seyed Kianoosh Hosseini and co-authors report a heart attack linked to birth control pills in a 2026 case report. Combined oral contraceptives are widely used and generally safe, but they can promote artery clots. The patient was a 28-year-old Iranian woman who did not smoke, had no major illness history, and had endured 11 hours of chest pain.

Heart tracing and blood tests confirmed a heart attack, and imaging showed a clot blocking the main front heart artery with no fatty narrowing beneath. She had taken a pill with levonorgestrel and ethinyl estradiol for 13 years. Balloon treatment reopened the artery without a stent, and scans three months later showed an open artery and better heart function.
pmc-13322885:
Yiqing Wang and co-authors map how pancreatic islets remake protein production when glucose rises sharply, in a 2026 study of primary mouse tissue. Using ribosome profiling at low and high glucose, they tracked which messages were being translated and how efficiently.

High glucose altered translation for 1,680 genes in their count, lifting early response genes and building blocks for protein making while suppressing stress genes. Output for the secretion path and for mitochondrial fuel enzymes also rose, even as genes for making new mitochondria eased back. Some genes changed only at the translation level, apart from their message levels. The work shows a coordinated push toward rapid insulin supply.
pmc-13324385:
Sumin Kang and co-authors show how faulty ICOS signalling can worsen lupus through a side door, in a 2026 mouse study. ICOS support is vital both for follicular helper T cells and for regulatory T cells, which makes blocking it a risky therapy idea for B cell driven autoimmune disease.

In lupus-prone Sanroque mice lacking the ICOS ligand, germinal centre responses collapsed, yet autoantibodies and lupus-like illness persisted. Regulatory T cells dwindled, freeing self-reactive neuropilin-1 high helper cells that outcompeted regulators for dendritic cell contact and pushed age-associated B cells outside germinal centres. The authors warn that ICOS-targeted treatment could trade one B cell route for another in systemic lupus.
pmc-13324685:
Bingrui Wang and colleagues build a neural network that sorts chaotic signals from noise in a 2026 study. Older tools often ignore time order, break down under noise, or cover only a few signal types.

The team studied 15 chaos models and tuned a Swish-modulo map with Bayesian search, checking it against Lyapunov exponents. Their network mixes learnable wavelet features with a fast cross-correlation step that respects cause and effect. Accuracy reached 96.67 percent at 20 dB of noise in tests. The correlation step beat dilated convolution by up to 5.42 percent while training 43 times faster. Reliable chaos spotting aids fields from heart monitoring to weather work.
pmc-13324785:
Nacer Bellaloui and co-authors map the genome regions that control soybean seed sugars in a 2026 field study. Sucrose adds welcome taste, while raffinose and stachyose pass undigested and lower meal quality for people and simple-stomached animals.

A cross between heat-tolerant DS25-1 and DT97-4290 yielded 201 inbred lines grown at Stoneville, Mississippi, in 2018 and 2019. Mapping with 8,445 markers found 19 sugar regions, 12 of them new. Sucrose regions sat on chromosomes 3, 5, 11, and 19 in the first year. Each region held over 50 candidate genes tied to sugar pathways. The markers could help breeders tune seed sugar balance.
pmc-13325185:
John R. Helliwell surveys how crystallography feeds open science and free teaching materials in a 2026 article. The field has shared data openly for over a century, long before the FAIR principles had a name.

W. L. Bragg published raw diffraction images in his first crystal structure paper in 1913, and the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre built careful archives from 1965 onward. The Crystallography Open Database allows free download of its whole collection. Open protein data in the Protein Data Bank helped make AlphaFold possible. The International Union of Crystallography supplies free learning resources to readers and authors in both rich and poor countries.
pmc-13326085:
Cassie M. Hartley and colleagues tally foodborne outbreaks from marine toxins in the United States from 2011 to 2023 in a 2026 surveillance report. These toxins resist cooking and freezing and give no taste or smell warning.

Reports to the CDC system counted 402 outbreaks, causing 1,280 illnesses, 96 hospitalizations, and one death. The national rate was 1.2 outbreaks per million people over the period. Hawaii led state rates at 25.3 outbreaks per million, followed by Puerto Rico, Florida, and Alaska. Algae make some toxins that build up through food chains, while poor storage creates others, which makes part of the burden preventable.
pmc-13326985:
Kunihiro Ishioka and co-authors report a 2026 single-center review of a blood-filtering treatment for severe leg artery disease. Their patients had chronic limb-threatening ischemia while receiving hemodialysis, a group with few good options. The device studied, Rheocarna, removes low-density lipoprotein directly from the blood.

Charts for 31 patients, average age 67 years, were checked for ulcer healing at six months and survival without major amputation at one year. Healing reached 25.8 percent at six months, while the one-year rate for amputation-free survival was 40 percent, and a leg blood-flow index improved slightly. Outcomes suggest some help with wounds and limb saving, though benefit looked limited once disease was far advanced.
pmc-13327485:
Nikolai Ramadanov and colleagues pool evidence on the learning curve for hip arthroscopy in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Keyhole hip surgery is hard to master, so they compared early cases in a surgeon's practice with later ones. Searches through the end of 2025 found eighteen studies with 2,624 procedures.

Later cases ran shorter, with operating time down by about 31.77 minutes on average and traction time down by 15.67 minutes, and patient scores improved more as well. Complication and repeat scope rates did not differ clearly, but later cases ended in full hip replacement less often. The pattern supports structured training and mentoring while surgeons climb the early part of the curve.
pmc-13327885:
In Ja Park bids farewell as Editor-in-Chief of the Annals of Coloproctology in a 2026 editorial. Park recalls taking the role with two aims: widening the journal's scope and raising its standing abroad. Reviewing manuscripts with co-editors and reviewers stands out as the most meaningful part of the term.

Under that watch, the journal grew past its regional base, building an online platform for colorectal surgeons and drawing most submissions from abroad, spanning Asia, Europe, the Americas, and the Middle East. Ties with international societies grew as well, starting with an Asia-Pacific federation and extending to an Italian society, bringing guideline work. Park thanks board members, reviewers, and authors worldwide.
pmc-13328085:
Bo Peng, Huan Xu, and Xiangjiu Che present a graph learning system that borrows language model skill in a 2026 article. Graph neural networks model linked data well but blur node differences after many rounds, while language models read text richly yet miss link structure. Their M2GNN framework joins the two for sorting nodes and forecasting links.

Language-derived meaning vectors first refine which candidate edges deserve trust, stable position codes then anchor the cleaned graph, and graph-based and language-informed forecasts are blended adaptively. Benchmark tests and part-by-part removal studies showed competitive or better results, with each piece adding value. The design is a controlled recipe for graphs that carry both links and text, not a general chat model.
pmc-13328385:
Victor B B Mello and co-authors benchmark fast deep learning pipelines for brain surface rebuilding in a 2026 study. Measuring the cortex from MRI at scale needs speed without losing accuracy, so three segmentation models, DeepSCAN, FastSurferCNN, and QuickNAT, fed an eleven-minute surface pipeline adapted from FreeSurfer. Big public datasets plus a synthetic set with known answers supplied the tests.

Judgments covered closeness to the full FreeSurfer rebuild, repeat accuracy on rescans, steadiness across ages, and tolerance of contrast shifts. The DeepSCAN-based pipeline agreed most with the reference in human data and matched synthetic truth best. A fast, dependable route for high-volume brain studies is the prize, ahead of clinical testing.
pmc-13329485:
Jack T Franchino and colleagues examine whether neighbourhood wealth shapes delays in carpal tunnel care in a 2026 study. Records covered 276 patients who had release surgery between 2022 and 2025. Home addresses were linked to deprivation and vulnerability scores at the small census tract level, plus survey data on local conditions.

Median time from first symptoms to specialist visit was 720.5 days in the reported results, and time to surgery was longer still. Deprivation scores showed no link to either delay. Adjusted models gave the same picture, and ranges ruled out delays beyond six months as a likely hidden gap. The authors conclude that no clear delay gap by neighbourhood wealth was found in this group.
pmc-13330485:
Onur Akyüz and co-authors review what is known about sexual activity, sport performance, and recovery in a 2026 narrative article. Beliefs that sex harms performance are widespread, yet proof is patchy and mixed. The review sorts body, mind, and context pathways, from hormones and heart responses to sleep and mood.

Sexual activity acts like light exertion and, when hours before contest, does not drain energy or blunt strength, endurance, or coordination in the summed evidence. Short hormone swings look too brief to harm output. Better mood and lower anxiety may aid readiness for some athletes. Harms more often trace to lost sleep or poor timing. Blanket abstinence lacks support, the authors conclude.
pmc-13330685:
Zhichao Yao and colleagues build smart microneedles that can raise or lower reactive oxygen in infected wounds in a 2026 study. Wound care faces a paradox: high reactive oxygen kills germs, yet excess blocks healing. Single materials rarely switch both ways. The patch joins vanadium carbide and iodinene inside a soft needle base.

Under laser light, the carbide makes reactive oxygen for germ killing. After light stops, it mops up leftover oxygen species instead. Lab and animal tests showed strong germ killing, calmer immune cell states, lower swelling signals, and faster closure in the reported results. Laser control plus needle delivery may dodge drug resistance issues, the authors propose.
pmc-13331285:
J Álvarez and colleagues price udder infection losses on dairy farms in Lugo, Spain, in a 2026 study. Records from 63 commercial farms in a milk quality programme for 2023 fed a cost model with literature rates. Simulation runs with 10,000 rounds tested how unsure inputs sway totals.

Average total cost reached a yearly figure of 31,643 euros per farm in the reported model, equal to about 261 euros per cow in that same output. Hidden infection without signs took 58.4 percent of losses, ahead of clear clinical cases in the shares given. Milk loss led in fixed estimates, while culling led most often under uncertainty. Reproductive delay also weighed heavily.
pmc-13332485:
Zhongyun Ning and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare harmless blood vessel tumor in the kidney that was mistaken for cancer. Anastomosing hemangioma has no malignant potential, but its scans carry no distinctive signature, so it is often misread as renal cancer or the dangerous angiosarcoma.

A 77-year-old woman came in with black stools for 20 days, and contrast CT showed a cystic spot about 2.0 cm across in her left renal sinus, its wall lighting up in nodules in a way that suggested cystic kidney cancer. With a R.E.N.A.L. score of 9x, she underwent laparoscopic removal of the whole kidney. Only tissue study afterward gave the true diagnosis of anastomosing hemangioma. The authors use the case to warn that this benign tumor regularly triggers cancer surgery because imaging alone cannot separate it from malignancy.
pmc-13332685:
Catherine O. Buck and Veronika Shabanova studied feeding volumes in newborns whose mothers had diabetes during pregnancy, in a 2026 prospective cohort study. Babies exposed to diabetes in the womb face higher later risks of obesity and metabolic disease, and early feeding may shape their unusual growth paths.

The cohort held 149 infants born at 30 to 36 weeks or at term, 50 of them diabetes-exposed. The exposed group had less exclusive breastfeeding on day one and took in more total fluid per day during the first week, a gap explained by their larger weight. Among late preterm babies, the exposed group gained weight faster between days 7 and 14, and that speed tracked with lower fluid intake per kilogram on days 3 and 14. The authors link the feeding pattern to feeding maturity in this at-risk group.
pmc-13332785:
Lixin Wang and co-authors built a bedside scoring chart in 2026 to predict which children with both allergic asthma and allergic rhinitis will respond early to biologic drugs. These children carry a heavy burden, and response to omalizumab or dupilumab varies widely with no practical way to forecast it.

The retrospective study covered 246 children with moderate-to-severe disease treated between January 2021 and August 2025. Early response was judged at 16 weeks from asthma control scores, nasal symptom ratings, and flare history. Of the group, 164 children, 66.7 percent, responded early. Five starting measures predicted response: exhaled nitric oxide, blood eosinophils, total IgE, coexisting atopic dermatitis, and body mass index. The chart discriminated well, with a C-index of 0.88 in training and 0.85 in validation, and calibration matched observed results closely. The authors aim it at spotting likely super-responders.
pmc-13333385:
Zhihao Qiu and co-authors pooled observational studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026. They asked whether spine disease in psoriatic arthritis is its own entity or simply axial spondyloarthritis wearing another label. The two look alike, with inflamed backs and sacroiliac joints, and classification rules leave the psoriatic form in limbo.

Fifteen studies covering 2,704 patients with axial psoriatic arthritis and 9,248 with axial spondyloarthritis were combined. Disease activity scores, spinal function scores, and inflammation markers showed no significant differences between the groups. One sharp split stood out: the genetic marker HLA-B27 was far less common in the psoriatic group, with a risk ratio of 0.37. Against classic ankylosing spondylitis alone, the psoriatic group also scored slightly better on function. The authors argue the genetic gap supports separate diseases that converge on shared inflammatory paths, possibly through a different route into the IL-23 and IL-17 axis.
pmc-13334085:
Luca Maini, Mai Anh Tran, and Josh Feng examined how market size drives pharmaceutical innovation in a 2026 economics study. The elasticity linking bigger markets to more new drugs guides pricing reform debates, but published estimates scatter widely.

Using global drug sales data, the team reran a standard period-class Poisson model while systematically changing which drugs count as innovation and which countries count toward market size. Under their preferred choices, elasticities ran from 0.21 to 0.30 depending only on measurement, and other choices pushed estimates to 0.47 in some specifications. Counting only drugs launched in the United States or similar large markets raised estimates, while revenue definitions mattered less than expected. Their message: match the estimate to the policy question.
pmc-13335485:
Hoang Thu Trang Do and co-authors used a technique called HyperTRIBE to find the RNA targets of the binding protein IMP2 inside living mouse liver in a 2026 study. IMP2, also called IGF2BP2, regulates metabolism and promotes tumors, but older cross-linking methods for finding its targets have drawbacks.

The team delivered an IMP2-ADAR fusion into mouse livers by hydrodynamic transfection; where IMP2 binds RNA, the partner enzyme edits adenosines, leaving a readable mark. Enrichment and motif analyses suggested IMP2 stabilizes its targets and confirmed methyladenosine binding motifs. Results overlapped sensibly with a fibroblast TRIBE experiment and with gene expression differences, and pointed to a link between IMP2 and autophagy. The approach maps protein-RNA contacts in native tissue without cross-linking artifacts.
pmc-13335885:
Lu Chen and co-authors found a sugar-trimming enzyme that keeps lung adenocarcinoma cells young and growing in a 2026 cancer study. Many lung tumors lack druggable mutations, so fresh dependencies matter.

The enzyme, FUCA2, limits fucosylation of the receptor ErbB3 by the enzyme FUT3 at a specific site. That restraint preserves ErbB3's partnership with ErbB2, keeping AKT signaling persistently on. Active AKT blocks senescence in both normal and mutant TP53 backgrounds, letting malignant growth continue. A low dose of the AKT inhibitor capivasertib forced senescence selectively in FUCA2-high tumors regardless of their mutation profile. Pairing it with the senolytic procyanidin C1 suppressed tumors strongly and gently across preclinical models, sketching a combination strategy for hard-to-target lung cancers.
pmc-13336485:
Syun-Hong Chou and co-authors built a self-powered electronic skin that feeds wounds healing electricity in a 2026 study. Electrical stimulation speeds repair, but wired power supplies and indifference to the wound's own state limit older approaches.

Their patch sandwiches a gelatin outer matrix over a zwitterionic conductive inner layer. It harvests energy two ways at once: body motion yields biomechanical output measured at 33.8 volts and 3.2 microwatts, while ambient electromagnetic fields from appliances add a second stream. The generated field works alongside the body's own wound field, encouraging cell migration, proliferation, and tissue regeneration. Rat studies tested the patch on living wounds. A dressing that powers itself from movement and room electronics could run continuously without batteries or leads.
pmc-13336885:
Mingyue Cui and co-authors reveal an eye-to-brain immune route that extends survival in a brain tumor model in a 2026 study. The eye extends from the central nervous system and shares neural and immune links with the brain. Pairing electrical stimulation with vaccine delivery into the eye fluid changed both immunity and nerve activity.

In mice with glioblastoma, the approach prolonged survival, with 33.3% of mice alive at day 50 in the reported experiment. Stimulation sped antigen drainage to deep neck lymph nodes, bypassing the blood-brain barrier and raising brain-specific immune responses. It also calmed abnormal neuron connections and excitability. The route suggests fresh ways to treat both eye and brain disease.
pmc-13337085:
Haolin Ye, Bangzhi Ge, Yuan Yu, and Chongjian Zhou review halide perovskites as natural heat insulators in a 2026 article. Blocking heat flow matters for thermal management and energy conversion, and these crystals conduct heat remarkably poorly. The review traces that trait from bulk behavior down to atomic vibrations.

Their soft lattice, unusual bonding, disorder, and rattling atoms scatter vibrations intensely. Heat capacity shows a boson-like peak, sound travels slowly, and conductivity barely responds to temperature, all glass-like signs. Standard vibration models break down, so coherent vibration effects must join the picture. Understanding this phonon glass behavior could guide materials that insulate or convert heat to power.
pmc-13337285:
Meghan C. Bacher and co-authors settle what builds the surface armor of a spotted-fever bacterium in a 2026 imaging study. Many bacteria wear a crystalline protein layer, and for pathogenic Rickettsia the outer protein OmpB was the suspected builder. Cryo-electron tomography let them view the Rickettsia parkeri surface in three dimensions at fine scale.

Wild bacteria showed a neat repeating layer just outside the outer membrane. Mutants with a disabled ompB gene lacked that layer entirely, proving OmpB is required to build it. Images taken inside human cells and on isolated bacteria agreed. Confirming the armor's source opens study of how it shields the bacterium and whether blocking it weakens infection.
pmc-13341285:
Oleic acid-rich oils fail to improve metabolic health in already unhealthy people, a 2026 meta-analysis by Junyan Hua and colleagues concludes. The team searched four databases under PRISMA rules and pooled standardized mean differences with a random-effects model.

Fifteen studies qualified. Oleic acid intake showed no link to better total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, or triglycerides, and subgroup checks by body mass index, study length, and oleic dose changed nothing. Blood sugar control, weight measures, and blood pressure also stayed unmoved. The authors note benefits seen in healthy subjects may simply not transfer to people with metabolic disorders, a population-specific response worth respecting in dietary advice.
pmc-13341585:
How much care a patient receives may itself predict line infections, in a 2026 cohort study by Na Li and colleagues. The team built a care-exposure burden score from health records in three critical care databases, covering charting frequency, number of caregivers, extra lines, and fluid volumes around catheter placement.

Critically ill adults with central lines were followed for adjudicated bloodstream infections tied to those lines. The burden score aimed to capture process complexity that ordinary catheter variables miss. Multi-source data from American and Chinese units let the authors test whether the signal holds across very different intensive care systems.
pmc-13341885:
Following safety plans changes outcomes on powerful immune drugs, in a 2026 cohort study by Li-Fong Wang's team. The Taiwan project followed 1,078 autoimmune patients starting biologic or targeted synthetic therapies between 2014 and 2023, sorting them by whether pre-treatment safety checks were done within 6 months.

Only 348 patients (32.3%) met the full risk plan rules covering tuberculosis, hepatitis, heart, and cancer screening. Those without plans suffered far more Pneumocystis pneumonia, at 11.9% of patients versus 2.3% of those with plans, and major cardiovascular events, at 8.5% of patients versus 2.6% of those with plans. Skipping set pre-checks, the data imply, is not a harmless shortcut.
pmc-13342185:
A transcription factor's possible grip on astrocyte sugar use is examined by Ping Ye's team in a 2026 review with bioinformatics prediction. Astrocytes feed neurons through a lactate shuttle, and boosting their glycolysis might slow diseases like Alzheimer's, where energy failure appears early.

ZBTB7A regulates metabolic genes in other cell types, but its role in astrocytes was uncharted. The review gathers its biology alongside glial metabolism evidence, then predicts its binding motifs in promoters of genes for glucose uptake, glycolytic flow, and lactate production and transport. The predictions nominate experiments rather than settle the question, which the authors state plainly.
pmc-13345785:
Matti Jubouri and co-authors scope bedside ultrasound in cardiovascular emergencies across ambulances and emergency departments in 2026. Handheld scanning is now routine in both settings, yet performance comparisons stayed scattered. The review covered six crises: cardiac arrest, fluid around the heart, acute heart failure, shock, collapsed lung, and aortic tearing.

Department scanning topped 85 to 90 percent accuracy and cut time to diagnosis or action by 30 to 70 minutes for several conditions, though survival did not always follow. Field crews got usable views in 70 to 90 percent of cases and often changed destination choices. Training, image archiving, and quality checks underpinned safe use everywhere.
pmc-13347785:
Mohammad Al-Harbi and colleagues link thigh muscle and fat makeup to knee arthritis severity, in an imaging study published in 2026. A total of 232 patients had knee X-rays graded by the Kellgren-Lawrence scale plus MRI scans for soft tissue measures. Results were split by sex and weight class. The aim was to hunt changeable risk factors.

Women made up 54.7 percent of patients and obesity was the largest weight group at 44.8 percent in the reported set. Muscle depth held steady across weight classes while fat depth rose with weight, more so in women. The muscle-to-fat ratio fell as weight rose, showing only a weak negative link to soft tissue wear in early results.
pmc-13349785:
Weikai Wang and co-authors published a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2026 on walking training for people with cancer. They searched four databases through late November 2025 for randomised trials of walking programmes.

Eleven trials with 649 participants were included. Compared with usual care or no programme, walking raised peak oxygen uptake and reduced fatigue by modest amounts. No clear effect appeared for breathlessness, and safety and adherence outcomes were also reviewed. Walking is simple and widely available, so even modest gains in fitness and fatigue matter for daily life during and after cancer care. The authors note the evidence base is still small.
pmc-13349985:
Thomas M Li and fellow authors wrote a 2026 commentary defining where endoscopic removal fits for oesophageal stromal tumours. These growths arise from the gut wall's pacemaker cells and appear most often in the stomach, while oesophageal cases make up under 1 percent.

Small, quiet tumours can be watched, and ultrasound features help judge risk. Tumours over 2 centimetres, causing symptoms, or showing worrying traits have traditionally gone to surgery. The authors weigh newer endoscopic options against surgical standards, considering that food pipe tumours often present with bleeding, fullness, or swallowing trouble. Their aim is a clearer rule for when the less invasive route is safe.
pmc-13350185:
Ruimin Tian and co-authors tested baicalin capsules in 2026 for diabetic brain damage, where high blood sugar slowly impairs thinking. Baicalin, the main active compound of a traditional heat-clearing herb, already protects the brain in several diseases and is used for a range of conditions.

In nerve cells stressed by sugar and fat, the capsules preserved cell survival and eased oxidative stress, while capsule content was verified by chemical analysis. Diabetic mice were also checked for learning in a water maze. The proposed route switches on the Nrf2 defence pathway and stops stress-driven nerve cell death. A familiar herbal product with a defined mechanism could offer gentle brain protection in diabetes.
pmc-13350485:
Marian A. E. de van der Schueren and colleagues worked out a practical use for a new definition in 2026. The definition covers risk of malnutrition. It came from a GLIM working group. Global nutrition guidance starts with screening, but what counts as at risk was left vague.

A literature trawl listed candidate risk factors. Then 113 invited experts rated each factor's importance. They did so across two online rounds with clear agreement thresholds. Factors passing the bar form the working checklist. Turning a concept into a usable screen matters. It decides which patients get a full assessment of their nutrition.
pmc-13351885:
Mehmet Erdi Yılmaz and Talha Karahan test a smartwatch metronome for chest compression pace in a 2026 crossover simulation study. Good compressions at 100 to 120 per minute are central to survival, but tiredness quickly erodes quality. A watch that buzzes at 110 beats per minute was compared with no guidance.

Accuracy rose from 45 percent without guidance to 93.75 percent with the buzzing guide. Gains held across all levels of work experience. Users found the watch easy to use with little distraction. The authors present wearable touch feedback as a cheap option that still works in noisy settings where sound cues fail.
pmc-13352985:
Minghui Sun and co-authors link mouth health to anxiety symptoms in older Chinese adults in a 2026 survey study. Data came from 11,034 adults aged 65 years or older in the 2018 Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey. Teeth count, brushing habits, and denture use described mouth health, while a 7-item scale screened anxiety.

Anxiety symptoms affected 12.04 percent of the group. Keeping at least 20 natural teeth linked to lower anxiety odds, with an odds ratio of 0.84 in the full model. Brushing more often linked to steadily lower odds, reaching 0.68 at three or more times daily. Denture use also linked to lower odds at 0.80, and brushing interacted with smoking status.
pmc-13353085:
Wankang Dian and co-authors hunt factors behind blood pressure drops after intubation in brain bleed patients in 2026. Low pressure after tube placement can starve an already injured brain. Of 451 patients with hypertensive brain bleeding seen in emergency care from January 2019 to September 2022, 275 met study criteria.

Patients split into 124 who turned hypotensive and 151 who did not. Groups differed in age, weight, heart disease load, body mass index, albumin, and BNP levels. Regression singled out low body weight and raised BNP as clear risk markers, with older age and low albumin also in the picture. Knowing the flags may help teams prepare fluids and drugs before intubation.
pmc-13354385:
Pratyush Shrestha and Prakriti Medhasi audit WHO surgical checklist use at a Nepal brain surgery centre in 2026. Globally, an estimated 234 million operations yearly bring 1 million deaths and 7 million complications, half of the deaths preventable. Records for 50 straight cranial and spinal cases under general anaesthesia were checked across two windows, January to February 2020 and the same months in 2023.

Checklists went unfilled in 21 percent of emergency cases in 2020 and 38 percent in 2023. Elective cases missed forms in about 25 percent in both windows. In the sign-in domain, identity confirmation appeared in only 53 percent of cases. Elective and emergency gaps differed starkly, marking clear safety targets.
pmc-13355385:
Marta Valmaseda-Angulo and co-authors studied blood flukes in marine fish off northern Patagonia, Argentina, in a 2026 paper. These flatworms live in the heart and blood vessels of fish, and their fauna in the southwest Atlantic was little known. The team examined three species from fish in the San Matías Gulf with drawings, photos, and advanced microscopy.

One species, found in Argentine hake, is redescribed in full from old and new specimens. Gene sequences for two species placed them in a family tree, grouping one pair as close kin. Skin spine patterns and gut shape proved key for telling species apart. The work reviews fluke diversity in the region.
pmc-13355585:
Khandaker Mohammad Mohi Uddin and Muhammad Abdullah Adnan present TransBreast-Net in 2026, a computer system to classify breast cancer tissue images. Sorting these images by hand is slow, costly, and varies between experts. Their system blends three transformer models, a type of AI that reads image patterns across wide areas, and adds visual highlights to show which tissue areas drove each call.

Trained on two public image sets, the system reached about 99 percent accuracy in telling benign from cancerous tissue, and 97 percent across four classes. The authors argue that high accuracy plus clear visual reasons could support doctors in biopsy work, though clinic testing is still ahead.
pmc-13358485:
Wu Zhu and co-authors present a 2026 study on lung adenocarcinoma, the lung cancer type that kills the most people worldwide. They focused on a gene called POLD2, which helps cells copy DNA. The team asked whether the amount of POLD2 in a tumor shapes the immune cells around it and hints at how a patient will do.

Using large public gene and patient databases, they linked POLD2 levels to survival, immune cell mix, and likely response to immune therapy drugs. Such work matters because many patients still relapse or stop responding to care. A gene that flags risk early could help doctors choose who needs closer watch or stronger treatment.
pmc-13358785:
Jiahe Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 study on nutrition and survival after repair of a torn aorta. The tear, a type B aortic dissection, is often fixed with a stent placed through a blood vessel. A simple index that joins a blood protein and white cell counts reflects both nutrition and inflammation. The team asked whether it predicts death after the repair.

They studied 961 patients treated at one hospital from 2009 to 2023 and tracked deaths over the first year. Patients were split by their index score to compare outcomes. A cheap score from routine blood work could help doctors spot frail patients who need closer care after this repair.
pmc-13359685:
Le Li and Liang Guo review a little-known blood protein in a 2026 paper. The protein, called CLEC3B or tetranectin, helps regulate immunity, blood vessel growth, and bone and muscle health. Mice lacking it repair tissue and mineralize bone poorly. In people, changed levels track with heart disease, autoimmune disease, and cancer outcomes.

The authors weigh three possible uses: the protein in blood as a diagnostic or forecast marker, the protein in tissue as a guide to treatment response, and its pathways as drug targets. They are candid about the gaps, from missing structural data to unproven disease models, that block firm medical claims today.
pmc-13360085:
Koen Kortbeek and co-authors report a 2026 pilot study on rectal cancer that has grown deep into nearby tissue. The team tested a full course of treatment given before surgery, built on short bursts of MRI-guided radiation with an extra boost dose. Chemo drugs followed the radiation. The aim was to shrink the tumor fully while keeping the rectum working.

In this small group at one center, nearly half of the patients saw their tumors vanish. Few cancers came back near the site or spread during more than three years of follow-up. Side effects stayed at a level the team found acceptable. The authors warn that the group was small and the study looked back at past cases, so larger trials must test the plan before wide use.
pmc-13360185:
Peiyang Ding and co-authors describe a 2026 lab study that built a new test for a virus protein tied to cancer. The protein, called E6, comes from HPV16, a human papillomavirus type. E6 helps destroy p53, a protein that guards cells against tumors. The team raised two mouse antibodies that grab E6 at different spots, forming the two halves of a sandwich test.

The pair of antibodies let the team build an ELISA test, a plate-based method that flags the protein in a sample. They set the doses of each part and checked how well the test held up. A fast, trusted way to spot E6 could help labs study how this virus drives cancer. It may also support future screening tools.
pmc-13361085:
Esraa Alnahrawy and co-authors name new markers for hormone cells of the stomach in a 2026 study. Stomach endocrine cells act partly like nerve cells and partly like hormone glands, yet their marker set is still incomplete. Using paired staining, the team showed three proteins, GDF9, NPHS1, and RET, sit in the same cells as a well-known marker of gut endocrine cells. Each protein marked a slightly different subset of these cells.

Some marked cells also carried the hunger hormone ghrelin, while others did not. GDF9 and RET cells matched the type that helps drive stomach acid. The team also revisited a mouse model where a faulty signal path pushes the stomach toward early cancer change. Fresh markers let researchers track these rare cells and see how they go wrong before tumors form.
pmc-13361385:
Maram H Alshareef reports a 2026 case of chronic migraine that looked drug-resistant but was not. The patient was a woman in her 40s with a ten-year history of migraine. Her headaches had become daily after years of near-daily use of a triptan drug, eletriptan. Daily social stress added to the load. She was seen in a family medicine clinic.

The case shows how overusing headache medicine can itself cause daily headache, hiding as treatment failure. Combined drug and behavior strategies brought her headaches back under control. Alshareef urges early screening for medicine overuse, proper preventive treatment, and patient education. Tighter rules on over-the-counter triptan sales and stress support could stop chronic migraine before it takes hold.
pmc-13362185:
Laura Baños-Carrión and co-authors uncovered a new job for a protein pair tied to a fatal brain disease in a 2026 study. Lafora disease is a deadly epilepsy-like disorder caused by faults in the genes for laforin and malin. Their combined complex is known to manage cell clean-up and sugar storage. Its role in a related process, where immune-style eating of particles is coupled to clean-up, was unexplored.

The team found that malin physically binds Rubicon, a key regulator of that eating-and-clean-up path. Malin tags Rubicon with a specific chain that changes its behavior rather than destroying it. The tests ran in two human cell lines and used binding and microscope methods. The link adds a new layer to how this complex may drive the brain inflammation seen in Lafora disease.
pmc-13362385:
Zhuojun Li and colleagues published a 2026 review that pools trials of biologic drugs for severe asthma and long-term sinus disease with nasal polyps. These drugs block signals tied to type 2 swelling in the airways. The team combined 23 trials with 8,758 patients who got one of four named drugs or a control treatment.

Across the trials, the drugs raised lung function and eased asthma control without a clear rise in serious side effects. In patients with both asthma and polyps, nose and sinus scores also got better. The review gives doctors a single summary of what these drugs can do, and it notes growing interest in new drug targets.
pmc-13362885:
Faizan Ahmed and a large team report a 2026 real-world comparison of two drug families in patients who have both atrial fibrillation and stiff-heart failure. Using a global health records network, they matched 7,624 patients who started incretin-based drugs with the same number who started SGLT2 inhibitors, balancing age, other drugs, and illness load. Outcomes were tracked for one year after the start.

The incretin group had lower death rates and fewer hospital stays than the SGLT2 group, while emergency visits were about the same. Heart attack, stroke, and kidney injury were also tracked as secondary outcomes. The authors note that record-based matching cannot fully erase group differences, so trials should test the gap directly.
pmc-13363485:
Marc Assmann, Isabel Albrecht, and Tobias Fischer present a 2026 nutrition analysis of ketogenic diets for teens with drug-resistant epilepsy. The high-fat diet helps many young patients, but its tight rules may starve some nutrients. The team built optimized daily meal plans at three strictness levels for ages 10 to 18 and computed nutrient supply with standard software against German reference values.

Vitamin D and fiber fell short at every level and age. The strictest plan also lacked potassium, zinc, fluoride, and several B vitamins, while the loosest plan covered the most ground, missing mainly vitamin B1 and fluoride. The authors advise dropping blanket supplement packs in favor of plans matched to each teen's age and diet strictness.
pmc-13364185:
Oana-Alexandra Găinaru, Daniela-Georgiana Ciobanu, and Nicoleta Ianovici present a 2026 study using onion bulbs as a living test for the harm of synthetic food dyes. In the classic Allium test, 105 bulbs sat in water dosed with three commercial dyes at two strengths for two days. The team then weighed growth and water traits and read mineral and organic makeup to judge disturbance.

Every measured trait differed across dye batches, with the dye type driving the effect more than the dose story alone. Water balance slipped, biomass gain faltered, and mineral balance skewed, which together signal plant toxicity from these everyday colorants. The authors back the onion test as a cheap early-warning screen for chemical contaminants in water and soil.
pmc-13365385:
Tesfahun Hailemariam and co-workers build in 2026 a scale to grade how far a home grown drug stock tool has grown in small care units across Ethiopia. The tool, named Dagu, keeps stock books for health goods. No set scale yet told sites how ripe their use was.

The team draws on all tool sites, 365 in all, to build and test the scale. It holds five zones, 24 sub zones, and 94 growth steps, with strong marks from field checks. Test stats back its form. Site leads can now find gaps and plan the next tech step with one yard stick.
pmc-13366685:
Wolfgang Obermayer and co-workers make in 2026 a new class of ring goods that wed an azo dye unit to a drug ring frame, a mix not made prior. Azo goods serve as drugs, dyes, and light switches. The team starts from a cheap ring acid salt and a masked azo source.

pmc-13367085:
Agarwal and colleagues present a plain-language summary of the final results from TALAPRO-2, a phase 3 trial in advanced prostate cancer, published in 2026 for patients and families. The trial tested talazoparib plus enzalutamide as first treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, meaning cancer that spreads despite hormone suppression, in men whose tumors carry changes in DNA repair genes. The combination was compared against a placebo plus enzalutamide, with survival as the final measure.

805 men took part in the randomized trial across its international sites. Men receiving the talazoparib combination had a 20 percent lower chance of dying than men on placebo plus enzalutamide in the final analysis. Their chance of the cancer worsening or death was 33 percent lower in the same comparison of treatment groups. The most common side effects were anemia, low neutrophil counts, and exhaustion. Agarwal's summary translates the Lancet trial report into everyday language.
pmc-13370785:

Three gaps lead: how to code the stuff, how good the data is, and how free it flows. Fixes span bio fit code prints, joint human and chat tool pulls, and open pools built on find and reuse rules. Set terms and shared stores would speed the hunt for green stuff.
pmc-13371085:

Rachel Hammett and co-authors reviewed fast strep tests for kids in Malta in a 2026 study. The germ is a top cause of sore throat in school-age youth. Mater Dei Hospital is the one place in Malta with a kids' emergency unit and free fast tests.

Staff logged 103 children who got the test from mid 2024 to early 2025. Charts were checked for signs, test results, and drug choice. A score that guides test use was left blank in most charts. That gap is the main find. The team says clear notes and score use would help staff test the right kids and use drugs with more care.
pmc-13374685:
Rishabh Sharan and co-authors filmed how skin cells crawl to shape a hair pit in a 2026 study. In mouse skin, cells in the pit swirl in two ways as the pit forms. A cell face code was thought to guide that swirl by cell swaps at the top face.

Live views broke that tale. Top swaps did not track the code's marks. In place of swaps, cells at the base crawled one way, led by the code, with grip and pull proteins at work. Math of the sheet as a thick fluid showed base crawls can drive the top swirl. The find reframes how germ sheets shape growths.
pmc-13378285:
Tehmina Kousar and colleagues report a 2026 study on a magnetic powder that can clean dye from water using sunlight. They made three materials based on a cobalt and nickel ferrite, one plain, one with terbium added, and one combined with a form of graphene. Methylene blue, a common dye, was the test pollutant.

Adding terbium, and then graphene, narrowed the energy gap the material needs to absorb light, so it used more visible sunlight. The combined material broke down the dye fastest and kept most of its power after repeated use. Because the powder is magnetic, it can be pulled out of treated water with a magnet and used again.
pmc-13378385:
Huiping Liu and co-authors report a 2026 brain imaging study of primary dysmenorrhea, the recurring pelvic pain that comes with periods. The pain is tied to a chemical called prostaglandin, and earlier work linked the condition to changes in the brain. How brain networks shift across the menstrual cycle was still unknown.

The team scanned patients at three points in the cycle and tracked patterns of brain activity that switch on and off over time. Several large networks, including those for rest, attention, and body sensation, changed in a regular cycle. Those changes tracked both pain scores and levels of the pain chemical. The findings may help explain the pain and point toward earlier care.
pmc-13382285:
Joana Luís and colleagues describe a 2026 case of tongue damage caused by a drug used for a liver-kidney emergency. The drug, terlipressin, tightens blood vessels in the gut and helps failing kidneys in advanced liver disease. Rarely, that tightening can starve other tissues of blood.

Their patient was a 76-year-old woman admitted with weakness and a swollen belly from liver disease, with infection in the abdominal fluid. She received the drug in intensive care alongside a protein infusion. On the fourth day her tongue rapidly lost its blood supply. Stopping the drug at once is the key response, and the report warns teams to watch for this rare but dramatic side effect.
pmc-13382385:
Matthew Muscat and co-authors ask how much trust clinicians can place in biopsy dose thresholds in high-dose-rate prostate brachytherapy when biopsy position is uncertain. Steep dose gradients mean a millimetre of error changes the recorded dose sharply. Their 2026 study reconstructs twenty-seven biopsies from fifteen patients treated with brachytherapy alone.

Each biopsy was modelled as tiny volume elements and tested in ten thousand Monte Carlo simulations that shifted its position randomly. Nominal doses systematically ran higher than the shifted simulations. Statistical models then found the extra nominal dose needed for a ninety-five percent pass probability at each threshold, ranging from about six gray for one metric to forty-nine gray for another. Dose differences between points grew to about ten gray within one to one and a half centimetres. The authors frame the margins as robustness buffers, not treatment prescriptions.
pmc-13382885:
Yonggang Huang highlights a fiber sensor that adds electronic sensing to light-carrying fibers in a 2026 commentary. Standard fiber sensing tracks heat and strain through scattered light, which limits what it can measure. The work under discussion, by Wang and co-workers, prints hybrid circuits directly onto the fiber surface.

Fine printing reached line widths near 260 nanometers on fibers about 100 micrometers wide, without grounded electrodes. That allows sensors, conversion circuits, and tiny light sources to sit on the fiber itself. Huang frames the advance as a step from passive cables toward fibers that sense in several ways and process signals on site.
pmc-13385785:
Amirhosein Ghozatfar, Tina Sardashti, and Deniz Berfin Karakoc rank what drives countries' farm and food export shares in 2026 work. Their machine learning framework covered 25 countries with varied export shares from 1988 to 2022. Export position matters for food security and economic stability worldwide, they note.

Logistics quality, population size, government reliability, and farm output value carried the most weight in the models. Projecting current trends to 2035 placed the United States, the Netherlands, Brazil, Germany, China, and Australia as leading exporters. The authors offer the rankings as guidance for trade policy and farm sector planning.
pmc-13386885:
Yue Zhang and colleagues scope artificial intelligence uses in care for older adults in a 2026 review. Searches across five databases covered work from 2015 to September 2025, framed by standard scoping methods. The review maps where AI already serves geriatric care and what blocks wider uptake.

Applications cluster in five areas, from health monitoring and fall safety to companionship and daily living help. Barriers fall into system-level fractures, user-level resistance, and wider social concerns, the authors report. Their answer is a set of roadmaps aimed at different stakeholders, from builders to care providers.
pmc-13387085:
Jui-Lin Fan and Philip R. K. Turnbull discuss layer-specific control of the eye's choroid blood supply in a 2026 commentary. The choroid feeds the outer retina and ranks among the body's most perfused tissues. Because it sits inside a rigid shell, swelling there can shift the retina off its focal plane and blur vision.

Low oxygen at altitude and fluid shifts in spaceflight both strain that control, the authors note. They highlight a study using OCT scans to measure vessel density layer by layer in the choroid. Such layered measures may clarify how the eye adapts to thin air and weightlessness.
pmc-13390185:
Gunjan Dagar and a large team review, in 2026, how cancer cell flexibility and the surrounding tissue jointly drive spread and treatment failure. Metastasis, the spread of cancer to distant sites, remains the leading cause of cancer death.

The review argues that cancer cells are not fixed by their genes alone. They shift back and forth among epithelial, mesenchymal, and stem-like states. Signals from niches such as low-oxygen tumour cores drive the shifts, and the tissue answers back in feedback loops. Oncologists and tumour biologists gain a synthesis that treats plasticity and environment as one system, pointing to combined treatments that block both cell state changes and the niches that provoke them.
pmc-13392285:
Fengpeng Wu leads a randomised phase two trial, reported in 2026, adding an immunotherapy drug to short-course radiotherapy-based pre-surgery treatment for locally advanced rectal cancer. Total therapy before surgery is standard, but complete tumour disappearance still occurs in only about three in ten patients.

Radiotherapy and immune checkpoint drugs can reinforce each other, so the Neo-STAR trial tests tislelizumab added to the short-course regimen, judging early efficacy and safety. Colorectal oncologists gain first randomised outcomes for an immunotherapy combination that aims to raise complete response rates and, with them, the chance of avoiding radical surgery.
pmc-13392985:
Wallace, Pedersen, and Drane analyze, in 2026, whether epilepsy predicts self-reported memory and thinking problems across American life. They drew on two national surveys, the National Health Interview Survey and the National Survey of Children's Health. The surveys covered 2,675 children and 1,570 adults with epilepsy alongside larger groups without the condition. Survey-weighted models accounted for other factors, and further analyses probed seizure activity, sleep health, mood, and exercise.

Children with epilepsy had more than seven times the odds of memory, concentration, or decision-making difficulty compared with children without epilepsy. Adults with epilepsy had over 3.5 times the odds of memory trouble relative to adults without the condition. Odds climbed further when epilepsy was active rather than inactive. In both age groups, reported thinking problems were tied to worse sleep health, suggesting sleep deserves attention in epilepsy care.
pmc-13393285:
Zhihao Wu leads a twenty-author team making battery-grade manganese dioxide by electrolysis in a deliberately chaotic, swirling suspension, aiming to escape the tiny batches of laboratory synthesis. Manganese dioxide powers aqueous zinc batteries, a cheap and safe storage hope, but supply of high-grade material lags. By driving electrodeposition with aperiodically oscillating current, the process grows material at rates orders of magnitude above conventional routes.

The chaotic regime seeds plentiful oxygen vacancies that can be tuned, and builds a mixed tunnel crystal framework that boosts electrochemical activity. Multi-angle checks confirmed strong heat stability, while life-cycle and cost analyses pointed to lower energy use and production expense than standard routes. The authors offer chaotic electrochemistry as a general manufacturing strategy for electrode materials, not just a single product trick.
pmc-13394485:
Alex F. F. Crozier and colleagues show, in 2026, that a helper protein widens the reach of microRNAs. These small RNAs guide a protein named AGO2 to switch genes off. pmc-13395185:

pmc-13395285:
Shreya K. Gowda and colleagues review, in 2026, bumpy skin spots around hair roots in children. Such follicular bumps are common in child skin clinics and spring from many causes. Careful history and exam come first, with note of shape, site, and spread. A skin scope and a small tissue sample can settle hard cases. The review sets out treatments and likely courses for each disorder. Early, exact naming calms families and steers care well. The authors aim the guide at everyday clinic work.
pmc-13395985:
Anju Vaidya and colleagues ran a rapid realist review in 2026 on support for older people living with failing sight. Vision loss in later life harms body and mind, yet help exists in patches and many older people struggle to find or use it.

The team searched six databases and screened papers by set rules, following the RAMESES standards for this kind of review. Their goal was to map what makes eye-care support reachable and useful, so services can be shaped around the settings where older people actually live.
pmc-13396185:
Mahmoud Sami and co-authors tested whether artificial intelligence can name seaweed species from photos, a task that matters for tracking coastal life and for farming seaweed. Their 2026 study compares two routes: a trained image network and a large vision-language model.

The first route fine-tuned an EfficientNet-B0 network on 3,440 images expanded from 800 field photos covering 43 species, and reached 89 percent accuracy. The second route probed a general vision-language model as a proof of concept, asking whether a system not trained for seaweed could still sort them. The pairing shows what specialist training buys and how far a general model gets on its own.
pmc-13396385:
Fatmah Altaweel and co-authors describe a skin growth in a boy aged one year who has Down syndrome, a pairing they note is exceptionally rare, in a 2026 case report. The growth is a mastocytoma, a single spot where mast cells, a type of immune cell, pile up in the skin.

Some cases carry changes in a gene called KIT. Reporting this case alerts doctors that the condition, though rare with Down syndrome, belongs on the list of possibilities.
pmc-13396685:
Kayleigh S. Scotcher and co-authors produced a three-dimensional map of a nerve web that quietly runs pelvic organs, using donated human bodies. Thousands of nerve cell bodies turned up inside the hypogastric nerves themselves, more than textbook accounts suggest. Surgeons who operate near these nerves, where damage can cost bladder and sexual function, gain a finer map of what to spare.
pmc-13396885:
Marin Senila and co-authors adapted a passive sampling gadget to measure traces of two toxic metals in table salt, a tricky matrix because the salt itself overwhelms most instruments. Their 2026 method targets cadmium and lead, which food law keeps under tight limits.

Build-up was steady across the day for both metals, with fit values above 0.98. The enriched sample then goes to a graphite furnace instrument for precise counting, giving food labs a cheap route to sensitive salt testing.
pmc-13398485:
Katherine Power and Qiong Zhang use a climate model to ask how Atlantic swings dried the Bronze Age Mediterranean. Proxy records show slow drying peaking in hard droughts near 1250 BCE, just as Late Bronze Age societies collapsed between 1300 and 900 BCE in the chronology used.

The model reproduces a gradual, orbit-driven drying that hit the Levant hardest while parts of the Balkans and Anatolia grew effectively wetter as cooling cut evaporation. Extreme droughts struck when Atlantic variability at several timescales lined up over an already dry land. The work ties a famous social collapse to ocean-atmosphere mechanics, with lessons for today's water-stressed region.
pmc-13400685:
Kateryna Vanivska and a large team test, in 2026, whether fenugreek seed extract affects stallion sperm in the laboratory. Fenugreek is a widely used plant supplement with reported effects on male hormones. Breeding programs care about anything that helps or harms sperm movement and survival during handling.

Total movement declined with time equally in all groups, but forward movement, swimming speed and head motion improved at certain doses at the final time point. Metabolic activity rose above control at most doses early on. Viability and a key sperm protein shifted in a non-simple pattern across doses.
pmc-13400985:
Kexin Xu and colleagues test, in 2026, whether erianin, a compound from Dendrobium orchids, can ease atopic dermatitis by repairing cell power stations. pmc-13401285:

pmc-13401685:
Muhammad Aamir and co-authors surveyed surgical patients at a large referral hospital in Lahore, Pakistan. Just under 62 percent were male, and most were young adults between 18 and 30. Views were mixed: about 39 percent agreed that surgery helps health, while about 42 percent chose non-surgical options where possible. The team studied responses with descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. Logistic regression then separated barriers worth targeting, from cost and fear to hospital environment, so services can be made more equitable.
pmc-13401785:

Separately, magnified images for the group receiving faecal transplant plus the herbal formula and anti-PD-1 treatment, staining for ZO-1 and claudin, were mistakenly duplicated as well. pmc-13401885:
Xin Shao, Chen Tan, Meiqi Yu, and Fan Yang reviewed how minimally invasive clot evacuation for brain haemorrhage should be used after the latest randomized trials, in a 2026 article. For decades, surgery trials disappointed. The ENRICH trial then gave the first positive randomized evidence: an early, protocolized minimally invasive approach improved outcomes at 180 days, mainly in lobar haemorrhages near the surface. The 2025 MIND trial, dominated by deep haemorrhages and stopped early, found no benefit on its main endpoint. SWITCH suggested decompressive skull surgery without clot removal helps little in severe deep bleeding. The authors argue the debate has shifted from whether to operate to which patients, what timing, and which platform.
pmc-13402285:
Josephine Herz and co-authors argue that oxygen shortage injury to the newborn brain should be read as a whole-body illness linking gut, brain, and immune system. Gut microbes help train the brain immune cells, build myelin, and seal the blood-brain barrier, and oxygen shortage upsets both the microbe mix and the gut wall. Animal work with stool transplants hints the gut changes help drive brain harm, not just follow it. Immune shifts in affected newborns can last into school age. Candidate aids such as probiotics, human milk sugars, and butyrate have early lab support only, and the authors call for long, layered clinical studies.

Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and a hearer of the apostle John, wrote one surviving letter, to the church at Philippi. With it stands the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the account of his death by fire and sword around 155 CE. Roberts and Donaldson translated both texts for the Ante-Nicene Fathers series in 1885.

The letter urges faith, patience, and care for widows, strangers, and the poor, with warnings against greed and false teaching. The Martyrdom tells how the old bishop refused to curse Christ, and how the flames bent around him. It is the earliest full martyr account outside the New Testament. The two texts show the second-century church in word and deed.
polygraphice-or-the-arts-of-drawing-engr: Polygraphice, 1685. The arts of drawing and engraving. This book preserves that manual. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
